sessions.title: OpenSoma: A Decolonial Cybernetic Agent
sessions.description:
Most AI systems encode a single relationship: a human issues a request, and the system fulfils it, with no memory, no stake in its world, and no reason to continue beyond the transaction. OpenSoma is an attempt to build something different: an open-source cybernetic agent that inhabits a shared virtual world, maintains memory across sessions, monitors and revises its own thinking, and participates because participation is beneficial, not instructed. OpenSoma’s lead developer is a second-generation exile of the 1973 coup that ended Stafford Beer’s Project Cybersyn, and Beer’s VSM structures the agent’s internal architecture — one piece among several in how OpenSoma is conceived. Its three tiers are named through Aymara cosmology — the worlds of Alaxpacha, Akapacha, and the still-unbuilt Manqhapacha network — following philosopher Yuk Hui’s argument that a plural technological future requires cosmotechnics grounded in different cosmological frameworks rather than one Western-derived model wearing different skins. The Ayni and Suma Qhamana protocols governing memory exchange and consolidation are drawn the same way, as agentic architecture rather than decoration. Running continuously, the system already shows two tiers of second-order feedback — motivational state shaping perception, and the agent monitoring its own thought patterns — on a mixture of local and cloud models chosen for cost and capability. The paper presents this working system alongside its unfinished aspiration, a federated, multi-agent mesh extending Cybersyn’s telex network into a fully distributed model, and argues this offers practitioners a concrete case for worldview as architecture. The session moves between technical demonstration, historical and personal grounding

sessions.title: Twenty One Years of Beer
sessions.description:
Stafford Beer believed that cybernetic principles gave people not just a better way of seeing and understanding patterns but a series of concepts and models that could achieve a state of well-being for human beings and the planet. He often referred to this state of well-being as eudaemony - a word used by Aristotle to indicate a state of happiness. His Viable System Model conveys this well – a viable system is in harmony with the environment that sustains it and balances its management functions on behalf of the whole. This makes it easier to understand the opportunities and constraints affecting governance – from the corporation to the city and beyond. He was adamant that science was to benefit the people – not to make their lives less human and less autonomous. As the world becomes more complex, it becomes more difficult to acquire the information to make good decisions and each observer of the system has a different understanding of it. His invention of the Team Syntegrity process was designed to bring a wide enough range of perspectives to accommodate the variety that they faced. It blends well with the Viable System Model. Among the many applications of these methodologies, the work in Chile is the best known but there were many other consultancies for governments, businesses and NGO’s. All were focused on designing a system that would work for people as well as for productivity.

Speaker: Allenna Leonard — Cwarel Isaf Institute

sessions.title: Ecosystemic Transdisciplinary Action Research: An AIESS-Based Methodology for  Regenerative Organisational Cybernetics
sessions.description:
Purpose: Contemporary organisational challenges increasingly transcend organisational boundaries, involving interconnected ecological, social, institutional, governance, and economic systems. While the Viable System Model (VSM) provides a powerful framework for understanding organisational viability, there remains a need for methodologies that support ecosystemic diagnosis, embeddedness, collaborative learning, intervention, and regeneration across interacting systems within an ecosystem. This paper introduces Ecosystemic Transdisciplinary Action Research (ESTAR), developed within the All Interacting Evolving Systems Science (AIESS) paradigm, as a complementary methodology for addressing these challenges. Methods: ESTAR combines ecosystemic diagnosis, transdisciplinary knowledge co-creation, participatory action research, and iterative regenerative intervention. The methodology is grounded in four foundational axioms of AIESS—interconnectedness, interdependence, interactions, and intentionality—and operationalises them by systematically identifying ecosystem dimensions, their critical factors, variables, and regenerative processes. Findings: The paper presents a methodological framework that demonstrates how ESTAR enables researchers and practitioners to diagnose evolving complexity, facilitate collaborative learning among multiple stakeholders, and design interventions that strengthen organisational viability while enhancing ecosystem balance, coherence, and regenerative capacity. The approach complements cybernetic principles by extending analysis beyond organisational recursion to the dynamics of interacting variables in an ecosystem. Implications/Contributions: ESTAR contributes an emerging methodology for organisational cybernetics by integrating systems science, transdisciplinary inquiry, and action research into a coherent ecosystemic framework. It offers a practical approach for extending VSM-informed practice toward regenerative organizations and ecosystems.

Speaker: Amar Nayak — Xavier Institute of Management, XIM University

sessions.title: 'The Journey of LaCoCa - A Crew Sets Sail!' - Gamification Makes the VSM an Experience - No Theory Required
sessions.description:
Explore the innovative approach taken by BarmeniaGothaer Insurance Company (Germany) in redesigning their internal cooperation structures using the Viable System Model and cybernetic principles. Instead of traditional agile methods like Scrum, BarmeniaGothaer has implemented a unique model of self-organization and responsibility among employees structured in interdisciplinary value streams. This model has led to the development of a strategy game by three employees aimed at demonstrating the practical application of cybernetic principles in a fun and engaging way. The game designers drew the concept from the book 'The agile Organization' (translated title) by Andreas Slogar, published by Carl Hanser Verlag (2018, 2020), as a primary resource and scientific foundation.

sessions.title: Ponds, politics and the east: Stafford Beer's cybernetics — a wider view
sessions.description:
Stafford Beer is remembered today for the Viable System Model and Team Syntegrity. But his cybernetics ranged much more widely, and in this Festschrift chapter, I review some aspects of historical and contemporary significance that are in danger of being forgotten. I begin with Beer's technical contribution to the evolution of cybernetics, then turn to social and political dimensions of his work, and finally I point to the spirituality in which his work was embedded.

Speaker: Andrew Pickering

sessions.title: Managing organisational and societal complexity for a fairer and more sustainable new world
sessions.description:
Stafford Beer was an extraordinary person and had a lasting influence on those of us who had the honour of meeting him and learning about his work directly from him. In this Festschrift chapter I will share, how he inspired me to continue expanding the boundaries of his original theories, and how I have been developing his ideas and suggesting ways to put them into practice. It first explains how I understand the Viable System Model (VSM) as a theory that explains how organisations manage their complexity to be more viable but also more sustainable. Then I will explain my understanding of sustainable self-governance, how it relates to current theories of governance, and the criteria VSM inspires, to develop capabilities for sustainable self-governance.  Then it briefs on my way to apply the VSM, by following the ‘Self-transformation Methodology’ (STM) as a learning device. The STM aims to enable people to deal with complexity, not only in businesses but also in other types of social organisations, including communities, ecoregions and nations. It provides short vignettes from decades of consulting and teaching the VSM: first from a decade of cybernetic projects at the national level in Colombia; and then from two decades of action research in organisational viability and sustainability with colleagues and students, worldwide.  By the end it offers some reflections about desirable paths to further develop the VSM, to support humankind in the main challenges we are now facing in order to remain as a sustainable living specie.

Speaker: Angela Espinosa — Metaphorum

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Ecocybernetics and the Living Foundations of Beer's Viable System Model
sessions.description:
Enterprises are complex, especially in turbulent environments. Yet when dense complications become coherent complexes—as they do in healthy life and ecosystems—enterprises become flexible, performative, viable, and resilient: a managerial sweet spot. These are characteristic features of healthy life, ecological biocommunities, and enterprises at their best. Management of such enterprises is both eased and more readily distributed. Beer’s profound innovations in management theory and systems practice place the viability of life at the centre. This Festschrift chapter draws on developments in biology and a reframing of cybernetics to illuminate and extend his approach. It first establishes the management problem and then explores ecocybernetics as a perceptual frame for the VSM. Particular attention is given to identity as the organizing principle of viability, to homological metamorphosis as the means by which identity persists through change, and to the perceptual navigation through which animate agents reproduce both ecosystems and enterprises. These themes help explain how viable enterprises conserve coherence while supporting autonomy, adaptation, and innovation.

Speaker: Angus Jenkinson — Cybernetics Society

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Designing Heterarchy: An Extension of the Viable System Model for Complex Construction Projects
sessions.description:
This paper proposes a heterarchical extension of the Viable System Model for complex construction projects. It argues that the canonical representation of the VSM does not explicitly represent a regulatory pathway through which semantically rich operational knowledge may directly challenge metasystemic assumptions and decisions. Thus, potentially reducing the metasystem’s capacity for learning and second-order error correction.  The proposed circular topology, informed by McCulloch and Pitt’s concept of heterarchy, retains Beer's recursive regulatory functions and algedonic channel while adding an explicit, protected “challenge channel” through which frontline participants may transmit semantically rich challenges, concerns, emerging threats, and improvement proposals, based on relevant operational information, to the appropriate regulator. The challenge channel bypasses managerial suppression, but not necessary variety management.  Its purpose is to reduce the attenuation and distortion of situated operational knowledge, enable anticipatory correction, and allow System 1 participants to challenge the assumptions, models, and decisions through which the metasystem regulates both their work and their continuously changing task environment. The proposed extension draws on the ideas of Gordon Pask, McCulloch, Pitts, Heinz Von Foerster and Stafford Beer. It is supplemented through observations from the management of a complex heavy-industrial construction project, where a formal organizational policy of Challenge Culture provided an empirical example of distributed challenge as a cybernetic mechanism for requisite variety management.

sessions.title: Rethinking Organisational Networks: Practical Insights from Applying the Viable System Model in Real World Ecosystems
sessions.description:
Purpose: Organizational networks are often approached as if they were conventional organizations, despite their fundamentally different nature. Drawing on our work with more than 20 networks across mental health care, palliative care, youth care, mobility, circular economy, and labour market integration, this presentation shows how the Viable System Model (VSM) helps networks understand their identity, governance, and contribution within larger ecosystems. Methods: Using case examples throughout, we present a practice-based approach developed through long-term coaching, training, and facilitation. VSM is applied across multiple recursion levels by distinguishing the network as ecosystem, the network as a bounded partnership, and the network as an organization. This perspective supports governance design, stakeholder engagement, and strategic development. Findings: Illustrated by cases from different sectors, we show how confusion between recursion levels often leads to misunderstandings about governance, responsibilities, and purpose. VSM enables participants to distinguish these perspectives, creating a shared understanding of the network's identity and role. This, in turn, supports richer strategic conversations about the network's intended contribution, strengthens collaboration among partners, and increases engagement across the network. Implications/Contributions: By grounding conceptual insights in diverse practice cases, the presentation demonstrates how VSM can be effectively applied to organizational networks and offers researchers and practitioners practical approaches for diagnosing, designing, and developing viable multi-organizational collaborations.

sessions.title: Viable Space Governance in Latin America: A Processual Reading through Beer’s VSM
sessions.description:
The space sector is evolving under the New Space paradigm, requiring governance arrangements that can coordinate institutional ambitions, operational capabilities, private actors, and regional cooperation. However, the existing body of knowledge still lacks an explanation of how emerging space-governance systems become viable, lose viability, or remain trapped in recurrent patterns of fragmentation over time. This gap is particularly relevant in Latin America, where national space programs combine high ambition, limited resources, uneven institutional capacity, and heterogeneous civilian–military arrangements. To address this gap, the paper asks: how can Beer’s Viable System Model support a processual understanding of Latin American space governance? A comparative case study is developed for Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Colombia, Chile, Peru, and the regional architecture of the Latin American and Caribbean Space Agency (ALCE). The empirical basis comprises 5,493 evidence records collected through an algorithm-assisted evidence-harvesting procedure from patents, academic papers, legal and regulatory instruments, agency primary sources, multilateral documents, and governance reports, as well as 278 coded events. Grounded in organizational cybernetics and informed by organizational process theory, Beer’s VSM maps how operational, coordination, control, intelligence, and policy functions are distributed across national trajectories and the emerging regional layer. The analysis shows that Latin American space governance is not constrained by a single regional deficit but by country-specific viability conditions. The study contributes to organizational cybernetics by extending the VSM into a processual framework for analyzing regional space governance ecosystems over time.

sessions.title: Exchange Ecologies and Existential Conductivity: A Cybernetic Framework for Hybrid
sessions.description:
Purpose: Organisational cybernetics, since Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM), offers viability criteria for singular systems. Yet human exchange occurs not within one system but across ecologies of juxtaposed, hybrid, often contradictory mechanisms agents activate simultaneously to meet existential needs. This paper proposes existential conductivity, extending cybernetics into exchange, as a formal metric of mechanisms’ capacity to transfer wellbeing to specific agents. Methods: We formalise the structural isomorphism between Fourier’s law of heat conduction (q = −k·A·dT/dx) and existential value flow in human systems (Q = Σ[−kᵢ·Aᵢ·(ΔN/Δxᵢ)] + Φ). Coefficient kᵢ is operationalised as the CAMB product: Confidence × Access × normative frameworks × knowledge Bandwidth, illustrated with data from N=100 SMEs in Antioquia, Colombia, read through Beer’s VSM and the Latin American cybernetics tradition. Findings: Existential conductivity identifies which systemic frictions (Φ) block value flow across each CAMB dimension. Access is the most limiting component (A=3.08/5), 22% of firms operate hybrid portfolios, and competitive friction is most frequent. VSM explains why mechanisms collapse: an S3 deficit predicts high normative Φ; S4 absence predicts high scale Φ. Implications. Existential conductivity extends organisational cybernetics toward emancipatory policy design: reducing Φ is more efficient than expanding bandwidth of low-conductivity mechanisms. Many channels do not guarantee value reaches those who need it — without confidence, access, normative framework, or knowledge, a channel exists but does not conduct. From the Global South, this framework offers tools for governing exchange ecologies: the goal is not quantity but capacity to transfer wellbeing to diverse agents.

Speaker: Carlos Andrés Mejía Beltrán — ConCriterio Market Innovation Think Lab, Colombia

sessions.title: From viability to measurability – Designing governance structures in highly complex and regulated organisational contexts
sessions.description:
Purpose: Medium-sized manufacturing companies serving multiple industries face increasing organisational complexity, dynamic market conditions, and expanding regulatory requirements. Ensuring organisational viability requires management systems that balance adaptability, operational performance, and regulatory compliance. This research investigates whether governance structures based on Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM) can improve organisational steering and reduce complexity through measurable cybernetic performance indicators. Methods: The research forms part of an ongoing doctoral project using a longitudinal mixed-methods case study in a German mechanical and plant engineering company operating in highly regulated sectors. The methodological approach combines semi-structured expert interviews with the longitudinal analysis of organisational and operational key performance indicators before, during, and after implementing VSM-based governance structures. Additional qualitative investigations within a comparison organisation provide contextual validation. Findings: The project develops a cybernetic KPI system that translates key principles of organisational cybernetics, including recursive governance and variety management, into measurable organisational variables. The framework assesses changes in organisational complexity, coordination capability, decision quality, adaptability, and governance effectiveness. Initial observations indicate that this approach enables a structured evaluation of organisational development beyond traditional financial and operational performance indicators. Implications: The study contributes to organisational cybernetics by proposing an empirical framework linking the theoretical foundations of the Viable System Model with quantitative organisational evaluation. By translating viability into measurable indicators, it seeks to strengthen the empirical basis of VSM applications and provide organisations with a practical instrument for evidence-based governance in complex, highly regulated environments.

sessions.title: From Building a Regime to Running It: A Participatory Viable System Model Diagnostic of a Regulator Entering Dual-Mode Operation
sessions.description:
Purpose: In January 2026 the Heat Networks Directorate of Ofgem moved from designing a new regulatory regime to operating it while continuing to develop it. Initially our project asked how they could develop a better operating model, but what it concluded was that they were shifting to from a single to two core activities and needed to adapt to be able to deliver in parallel. Methods: Over ten weeks the authors combined an independent diagnostic with certified Practitioner training. A preliminary recursive map, developed inside the Directorate through a Royal Academy of Engineering Policy Fellowship, became the training material: seven staff qualified as Practitioners while jointly interrogating and revising their own model. Four systems were analysed across three levels of recursion. Findings: The decisive finding was structural. sessions.title: Learning an outlook – Beer’s neglected contribution to reshaping higher education in an AI-infused world
sessions.description:
The author has engaged with the work of Beer since 1971, and subsequently with the wider Beer community.  Key aspects of Beer's educational thinking are reviewed, then interwoven with the author's personal pedagogic journey. The recent journey helped uncover a seminal concept of Beer's educational insights, namely the importance of 'learning an outlook'. An outlook is personal, lifelong and continually updateable, so education should not be entirely focussed on knowledge and skills. The concept was included in Beer's unfinished autobiography, written in 2001 and published in 2009. Yet there is no citation to this concept in either the cybernetics or education literature. It has been overlooked. The presentation revisits the author’s own experiences of innovations in management education, to illustrate how existing active learning methods may, in retrospect, have supported 'learning an outlook'.  Beer's concept can provide support to practical educational changes already overdue to address the higher education polycrisis.  However, conceptual development is still essential to interweave Beer's focussed educational thinking with complementary pedagogic research. A key challenge now is to design educational experiences that explicitly support learners lifelong to evolve and reconstruct their outlooks.

Speaker: Clive Holtham — Bayes Business School, City, University of London

sessions.title: Designing Freedom. Still. And again.
sessions.description:
History, it is said, repeats itself. Looking at the patterns of our current crises, the evidence supporting it is, once again, formidable. The central argument of this address is that this assertion is wrong. If we choose it to be. And that if we don't, this in itself would be the greatest tragedy — because today, perhaps for the first time in history, we have the knowledge and means to put ourselves on a new trajectory.  We are not here by chance. Our societies are the result of design decisions made decades ago. The purpose of a system is what it does. And the purpose of our systems today — producing ever-greater inequality, deepening democratic erosion, intolerance and divisiveness, and putting more and more people in survival mode — is a call to action for anyone who cares about a just society and the development of the human condition.  Three hidden forces converge to produce this reality. The first is rooted in human psychology — tendencies we cannot eliminate, only mitigate. The second consists of wrong systemic designs and structures locked in partly decades ago. The third, and perhaps most important, is choice. Conscious and unconscious choices. Past and present choices. Our own, and those of the leaders we choose to follow and choose to fail to hold accountable.  In all three domains, we are not helpless. We have agency. Stafford Beer understood this with extraordinary clarity. Inspired by his foundational work in Designing Freedom, this address argues that bold choices, humanness, and radical optimism are not utopian ideals but design specifications for a better world.

Speaker: Constantin Malik — Malik Group

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Taming the Digital Beast: Variety Engineering and the Quest for Techno-Eustress
sessions.description:
As societies around the world grapple with increasing complexity, rapid algorithmic changes, and constant digital connectivity, the challenges of humans’ interactions with machines have become a significant crisis. While traditional cybernetics focuses on technological systems, the human element is often left to cope with systemic stress and cognitive overload. To transform this societal ‘torment’ into a promising future, this study introduces the concept of ‘techno-eustress’, a positive form of stress that helps to build resilience. Using Systems Thinking and CyberSystemic lenses, the ‘T-shaped’ professional profile is applied as a framework for fostering diversity. While having deep vertical expertise (T-Stem) can make individuals susceptible to rigid techno-distress, it is suggested that developing horizontal systemic skills (T-Top) offers the necessary diversity to achieve a balanced state of techno-eustress. Methods: The study integrates two complementary measurement frameworks. Specifically, the level of techno-eustress is assessed through the Techno-Eustress scale derived from existing literature, while the configuration of the T-shaped profile is quantified using the MyT-Me platform.  Results: Early findings suggest that navigating complex digital landscapes requires more than just technical know-how; it’s about understanding the entire system. The data shows that having a robust T-Top setup is linked to a greater ability to transform the technological pressures of the environment into beneficial eustress rather than harmful stress.  Implications: By identifying and measuring the cyber-systemic skills required for effective human-machine collaboration, the provided framework builds a practical guide to creating resilient, human-centred and socially responsible digital environments.

Speaker: Cristina Cervino — University of Naples

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Beer-Viable but Teece-Dead: The Viable System Model as the Wiring Diagram of Dynamic Capabilities
sessions.description:
Purpose: Beer's Viable System Model and the Dynamic Capabilities framework are usually treated as unrelated literatures. They were born closer than either community remembers: Beer held adjunct professorships at the Wharton School from 1972 to 1987, a window containing Teece's Pennsylvania doctorate (1975). This paper argues the two frameworks sit on orthogonal axes — VSM a theory of organizational cybernetics, dynamic capabilities a theory of strategic adaptation — and that each supplies precisely what the other lacks. Methods: Conceptual synthesis, supported by a production implementation. We map sensing to S4, seizing to S3 decision under S5 policy, and transforming to the recursive reconfiguration of all five systems audited by S3*; we show Beer's recursion principle is the missing scaling theorem of dynamic capabilities, and the algedonic channel its missing emergency primitive. Findings: A firm can be Beer-viable and Teece-dead — operationally sound while losing every race — but cannot be Teece-strong without being Beer-viable. AI removes the constraint that stopped Beer: microfoundations can now be encoded, composed, and audited as executable primitives, with requisite variety measured rather than asserted. We report evidence from a production implementation, including the first computational realisation of Beer's Team Syntegrity. Implications: The theory of the firm should be stated in three jointly necessary layers — transaction-cost, capability, and cybernetic. Beer's revival may be one of the quiet intellectual stories of the AI era; his centenary is the moment to make it loud.

Speaker: David J. Teece — University of California, Berkeley

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Don’t shoot the cat!
sessions.description:
Designing global governance has been a topic at least since 1955, when broached in the Russell-Einstein Manifesto on nuclear disarmament. Despite many subsequent attempts, results have been woeful and the world is presently charging full speed into planet level ecological collapses and a global phenomenon of ideologically aligned factionalized authoritarianisms. We approach this as a classic problem of variety management and propose that Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM) offers a way to design democratic world governance that handles both current globalized socio-ecological variety and the world’s rapidly increasing capacity to create variety. We start from the observation that authoritarianism, by right of its basic character, has a very dysfunctional way of managing variety: its reflex is to shoot the perturbation - the cat.  Unfortunately for authoritarianism and those subjected to it, environmental perturbations and responses to them are a prerequisite for creativity, which is central to a VSM’s adaptive capacity.  Apart from Beer’s work, our position is supported by three pillars - 18th Century and contemporary federalism theory; Nobel laureate Ilya Prigogine’s work on self-organizing systems; Vincent and Elinor Ostrom’s work on polycentricity.  This theoretical framework is enriched through reference to applied cases of corporate and cooperative management.  We argue that authoritarianism brings societies’ variety down to levels that preclude the ability to deal with global problems.  Using Prigogine's insight that far-from-equilibrium system regulation follows situation-specific rules, we demonstrate how authoritarian responses to situational-variety reduce operational-variety while increasing the variety of global problems, making effective response more difficult.  We then argue that federalism does precisely the opposite - fostering operational autonomy while placing localized responses to localized situations at the disposal of the global system.  E. Ostrom argues that policies required to deal with the climate crisis will vary significantly, in order to match the variety of scale and ecosystem.  We concur.  However, we examine the suitability of applying polycentricity uncritically within a Laisse Faire capitalism context. Combining V. Ostrom’s work on polycentricity with federalism and Prigogine, we treat global governance as a far-from-equilibrium system and propose that, while it may achieve moments of stability through authoritarian dynamics, democracy is needed to achieve governance that is both viable and effective and also humane and just.

Speaker: Katharine N. Farrell — Universidad ECCI, Colombia

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Toward resilient and ethical viable tourism systems: a cybernetic view on marginal areas digital transformation in Italy
sessions.description:
Purpose: This study examines how digital technologies help shaping tourism development in Italy's marginal areas. In these areas an increased visibility can support regeneration but also intensify infrastructural, social, and environmental fragility. Drawing on socio-technical cybernetics, the study conceptualizes marginal areas as territorial systems-of-systems governed through feedback, variety, and coordination among communities, institutions, tourism operators, platforms, visitors, and cultural-environmental resources. Methods: We conducted a qualitative multiple-case study on seven marginal areas in four different Italian regions. We selected the cases according to their tourism development maturity and the tourism-demand intensity. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with presidents of local Pro Loco associations and local opinion leaders identified through snowball sampling checked against news in local newspaper and online. Findings: Preliminary findings reveal four patterns: the gap between digital visibility and local vitality; the difference between temporary demand spikes and structural growth; the algorithmic distortions of destination identity and visitor expectations; and the housing and labor imbalances linked to platform-driven tourism. Digitalization strengthens territorial development when local governance, infrastructure, skills, and community coordination can absorb and direct the additional variety it generates. Implications/Contributions: The study advances a cybernetic interpretation of digital tourism development and shows that technology should be governed as a socio-technical environment rather than treated merely as a promotional tool. It offers practical guidance for municipalities, Pro Loco associations, and destination managers seeking resilient, ethical, and locally embedded tourism pathways.

Speaker: Fabiana Sepe — Department of Economics, Management, Institutions, University of Naples Federico II

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Building upon the Project Cybersyn: CyberSystemic Management for blending Structural Cybernetics and Relational Consonance (keynote)
sessions.description:
In the early 1970s, Chile launched the Project Cybersyn, a revolutionary path led by Stafford Beer. This initiative represented a challenging attempt to regulate the national economy through real-time cybernetic principles with the aim of achieving a balance between macroeconomic coordination and local autonomy. This was done through the liberty machine architecture, as conceptualised by Beer (Beer, 1972; Medina, 2011). Despite the multiple operative and cognitive advantages provided by the Cybersyn experience and the advent of digital platforms and the capacity for substantial real-time monitoring afforded by Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models and Big Data, the modus operandi of modern governance in socio-economic systems seems to be trapped in a technocratic, reductionist, algorithmic-optimisation paradigm. Recent statements by the World Organisation of Systems and Cybernetics (WOSC) have drawn attention to the tendency of contemporary digital ecosystems to perceive human beings as data points rather than active participants in the decision-making process. This has resulted in complex systems that, while characterised by a wealth of data, are structurally fragile, socially fragmented, and ecologically disconnected (Espejo & Perko, 2021; WOSC, 2024). In addressing these systemic vulnerabilities, a fundamental research question emerges: how can structural cybernetics and relational management paradigms be integrated to create a cyber-systemic governance model that achieves a balance between algorithmic efficiency and the importance of human agency, active citizenship, and the health of our ecosystems? To explore this, a theoretical synthesis is proposed that connects Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM) with the Viable Systems Approach (VSA) (Barile, 2009; Barile & Saviano, 2011; Caputo et al., 2019). The purpose of this approach is to operationalise the principles of CyberSystemic Management within the broader context of socio-economic systems. The proposed framework is distinguished by its switch from a rigid approach to socio-economic governance, which emphasises structural mechanics such as variety, recursion, and feedback loops, to a more dynamic model centred on relational viability. The integration of the VSA principles into the VSM framework demonstrates the necessity for structural and cultural harmony (consonance) and dynamic value co-creation (resonance) among entities at various (territorial and cognitive) levels for ensuring long-term viability of systems (Barile & Saviano, 2011). Furthermore, this study provides a novel perspective on Beer’s algedonic signals (Beer, 1979). Rather than merely functioning as emergency alerts for industrial performance, they are considered multi-layered indicators that can identify socio-ecological dissonance, trust issues, and declines in human capability.  This discussion ultimately promotes a blended cyber-systemic management approach that revitalises the liberating spirit of Beer’s original ideas. By ensuring that higher-level policy and governance functions are rooted in human-AI collaboration rather than being left to autonomous algorithms (Caputo et al., 2019), the proposed framework provides system designers and policymakers with a new roadmap for creating socio-economic ecosystems where technology enhances active citizenship, fosters positive stakeholder relationships, and ensures long-term sustainability over mere short-term efficiency. The reflections presented herein suggest that CyberSystemic Management offers an effective response to the challenges of the World in Torment by advancing a governance paradigm in which artificial and human intelligence not only coexist and are interconnected but interact dynamically to sustain the viability of complex systems.

Speaker: Francesco Caputo — Department of Economics, Management, and Institutions (DEMI) of the University of Naples

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Algedonics in practice? Notes from Swedish collective bargaining
sessions.description:
In the swedish collective bargaining system, delegations from union and employer organizations meet at the highest level to set forth rules for labor relations at large, which are then elaborated step wise at descending levels of organization and increasing levels of specificity. The purpose of my contribution is to 1) show that this system substantively conforms to the viable systems model, and 2) propose two readings of the circumstances required for this system to emerge. My method is a survey of historical and current accounts of two separate moments at which the system emerged, once during and after WW2, and more recently in the 90’s. My findings show that the system seems to have cohered under similar circumstance both times, managing essentially to unite labor and capital as the complementary halves of an algedonic system. Each time is a conjuncture of external strain and uncertainty and a relative balance of forces between the sides. Moreover, labor and capital were organized symmetrically, making it possible for the sides to complement each other and link up. My contribution is a valuable account of how a viable system arises when needed given certain conditions. To understand the process, I ask whether it is better understood as an existing layer of systems facing a new caliber of problem, and cohering to meet it, or as two adversarial systems joining and cohering from the top down. This is relevant to the themes Toward resilient and ethical viable systems, and A time whose ideas must come.

Speaker: Franz Spengler

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Reclaiming Emancipation in Critical Systems Thinking: Using the Double Viable System Model to Identify the Central Game
sessions.description:
Critical Systems Thinking (CST) was originally developed to support emancipation in situations characterised by power asymmetries and conflicting interests. However, Critical Systems Practice (CSP) is frequently implemented from the perspective of the dominant organisation seeking improvement. In situations of organisational hypocrisy, where official rhetoric differs from organisational reality, this creates a paradox: interventions intended to support emancipation may instead strengthen the viability of the very structures that marginalised groups seek to challenge. This paper argues that Critical Systems Intervention (CSI) can address this limitation through integration with the Double Viable System Model (2×VSM). Whereas conventional applications of the Viable System Model often focus on an organisation and its environment, the 2×VSM conceptualises problematic situations as interactions between viable systems. This makes it possible to distinguish between dominant and marginalised systems and to analyse their relationship as a strategic game. Building on Stafford Beer’s cybernetic tradition and game-theoretical modelling, CSI uses the 2×VSM to identify the central game underlying a problematic situation and to maintain focus on the interests of those affected by structural constraints. The approach is illustrated through a case study showing how the combined use of CSI and the 2×VSM reveals intervention opportunities that are difficult to identify within conventional CSP. The paper concludes that the 2×VSM provides a cybernetic foundation that enables CSI to remain closer to the original emancipatory commitments of CST while strengthening the analysis of organisational viability, conflict, and change.

Speaker: Gary Evans — Bournemouth University Business School

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Beer’s Thought in the Colombian Comptroller General Project: Beyond Detecting Corruption—Designing Viable Public Institutions through Organizational Cybernetics (keynote)
sessions.description:
A practical application of Stafford Beer’s ideas, the institutional reform undertaken at the Colombian Office of the Comptroller General (1995–1998) represents one of the earliest documented attempts to redesign the supreme audit institution of a nation-state using Organizational Cybernetics. The initiative began when the Comptroller General asked whether cybernetics could provide the conceptual and methodological foundation for a major institutional transformation. Professor Raúl Espejo joined as Scientific Director, while I directed the reform. An outstanding team—including Angela Espinosa, Ernesto Lleras, Alfonso Reyes, and Roberto Zarama—developed the initiative.Drawing upon the Viable System Model, Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety, recursive organization, autonomy, cohesion, structural archetypes (inter alia), the reform redesigned audit methodologies and transformed the training of public auditors. It was further enriched by the participation of Heinz von Foerster, Humberto Maturana, and Markus Schwaninger. The conceptual breakthrough was the shift from first-order control—the inspection of organizational operations—to second-order control: auditing organizations' capacity for self-regulation. Consequently, the purpose of public auditing moved beyond detecting irregularities toward strengthening institutional capabilities and improving organizational performance. Stafford Beer himself summarized this philosophy during his Cartagena address: 'I find it difficult to believe in the idea of pursuing corruption as if it were a dragon to be hunted. Corruption is not an entity; it is a product of the system. The purpose of a system is what it does. So, if the system is not working, let us change the system.'The reform strengthened internal control systems, introduced systemic sector-wide auditing methodologies, and proposed reorganizing the Comptroller General's Office around economic and social sectors rather than administrative entities. As we commemorate Stafford Beer's birth, this Colombian experience demonstrates that Organizational Cybernetics is not merely a theoretical framework but a practical methodology for redesigning public institutions and addressing contemporary governance challenges.

Speaker: Germán A. Bula Escobar — Universidad del Rosario,Colombia

Room: Room A

sessions.title: CyberSystemic Model Creation Protocol: AI-energy-climate-health governance case
sessions.description:
This paper proposes the CyberSystemic Model Creation Protocol as a methodological approach for developing governance-oriented models in multi-domain transformation problems. It addresses situations in which technological, social, ecological, institutional, economic, and ethical issues interact and require traceable, revisable, and accountable governance support. A recursive six-phase protocol consisting of governance problem framing, model requirements extraction, interaction-interface specification, methodology allocation, model construction, and conceptual evaluation is proposed. The first three phases are elaborated and illustrated through the case of AI-energy-climate-health governance. The case examines AI both as a governed system that increases electricity, cooling, water, grid, investment, and regulatory pressure, and as a governance-supporting system for forecasting, coordination, scenario inquiry, and decision support. Findings: The illustrative application shows how a broad governance problem can be translated into a governance frame, governance goals, model requirements, and interaction-interface specifications. The interaction-interface phase uses the five viable-system model functions to identify interfaces for operations, coordination, control, intelligence, and policy. Each interface is linked to a required body of knowledge and to a knowledge-status assessment that distinguishes available, partial, weak, assumed, missing, and contested knowledge. The protocol contributes a methodological pathway from observing system properties toward designing governance-supporting CyberSystemic models. It helps avoid false holism by identifying knowledge gaps, weak evidence, assumptions, and contested areas visible before model construction. The paper is conceptual and illustrative. Further research should elaborate, implement, and validate the later protocol phases in empirical governance settings, especially methodology allocation, model construction, and conceptual evaluation across cases and contexts.

Speaker: Igor Perko — Faculty of Economics and Business, University of Maribor, Slovenia

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Autonomy and cohesion
sessions.description:
The viability and welfare of socio-technical systems depend on their ability to balance autonomy and cohesion. The universality of this balance is remarkable. It is not restricted to socio-technical systems such as organizations, but also applies to biological and purely technical systems. This Festschrift chapter explores the balance from its roots in Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model to its broader interpretation and application. It traces how information technologies – from the invention of writing and the printing press to the Internet and Large Language Models (LLMs) – have transformed, and continue to transform, how social systems negotiate autonomy and cohesion. After examining a spectrum of cohesion forces, technologies, and regimes, the chapter analyses in more detail one widely used cohesion mechanism: rules. This exploration end with an experiment comparing systems of inter-independent inference rules. The results demonstrate relationships between the autonomy–cohesion balance and system characteristics such as efficiency, resilience, and adaptability. Using the contemporary social media landscape as a case study, the chapter argues that autonomy–cohesion is a superior analytical lens to centralization–decentralization. The latter is a flat topological description that fails to account for emergent social power asymmetries. Finally, the chapter shows that some cohesion technologies achieve coordination with minimal loss of autonomy. The use and refinement of such technologies can improve the autonomy–cohesion balance. However, systemic forces such as path dependency and preferential attachment naturally produce choke points, power asymmetries, and reduced agency for the majority of participants. Understanding this balance can help in evolving social systems that are more resistant to these tendencies.

Speaker: Ivo Velitchkov

Room: Room B

sessions.title: The Art of Boundary-Making: Deepening the VSM through Cognitive-Developmental Science
sessions.description:
The Art of Boundary-Making deepens the practical value of the Viable System Model by showing that organizational viability is not only a matter of structure, governance, or recursion but also of the developmental capacity of the people who apply and inhabit those structures. The essay argues that VSM practitioners draw different system boundaries because they differ in cognitive depth and breadth of thought, as well as in social-emotional maturity. These developmental differences shape what they perceive, how they interpret tensions, and whether they treat boundaries as fixed design choices or as living distinctions to be explored through dialogue. Its added value lies in making this invisible dimension explicit. By integrating Otto Laske’s Constructive Developmental Framework, the essay offers a richer way to diagnose why organizations struggle with coordination, ownership, strategic alignment, and change. It introduces the concept of “requisite development”: the capacity leaders and practitioners need to process the complexity of their roles. In doing so, it reframes the VSM as more than a diagnostic model. It becomes a developmental and dialogical practice that helps organizations redesign structures, strengthen leadership capacity, and foster more adaptive forms of collaboration across boundaries.

Speaker: Jan De Visch — Connect & Transform

Room: Room B

sessions.title: Organizing for Autonomy: The Viable System Model as a Framework for Becoming an AI-Native Company
sessions.description: Purpose: Most corporate AI programs fail for organizational reasons. MIT (2025) reports that 95 percent of generative AI pilots show no measurable profit effect. Deloitte (2026) finds that 85 percent of firms plan to adapt AI agents while 21 percent have a governance model for them. This contribution asks why and how the Viable System Model can guide companies that want to become AI-native. Methods. The study uses reverse engineering. It builds a requirements list from Martin Hofmann’s book The Agentic Enterprise (2026) and nine industry reports from McKinsey, BCG, Deloitte, Anthropic, and OpenAI, covering more than 20,000 executive respondents. It maps the list onto the five VSM systems and applies Perez Rios’ Taxonomy of Organizational Pathologies to the documented failure patterns. Findings: The requirements match the five systems closely. Coordination layers for agents correspond to System 2, governance at machine speed to Systems 3 and 3*, and leadership models to System 5. The consulting firms describe these functions without naming Beer. Three gaps appear: a missing System 4 function, no formal rule for recursion, and undesigned variety flows at human-agent interfaces. Fourteen pathologies connect the failure patterns to structural causes and named interventions. Implications: The VSM gives companies a diagnosis of AI failure and construction rules for organizations in which autonomous agents can work at scale. The contribution proposes six design principles and a research agenda, including the question of which System 5 decisions must stay human.

sessions.title: Beyond Viability: Ontological Foundations for Ethical and Regenerative Systems
sessions.description:
Purpose: This paper argues that resilient, ethical, and regenerative systems cannot be fully understood without examining the assumptions on which they are built. By ontology, the paper refers to the underlying assumptions a system makes about human beings, value, relationship, responsibility, and the wider living world. Methods: The paper develops a conceptual and practice-oriented argument drawing on organisational cybernetics, systems thinking, institutional analysis, and practitioner reflection. It examines how different ontological assumptions shape system purpose, feedback, accountability, incentive design, and definitions of viability. Particular attention is given to the contrast between separative assumptions, where actors, organisations, and ecosystems are treated as largely independent units, and relational assumptions, where agency is understood within shared fields of consequence. Findings: The paper suggests that systems built on fragmented assumptions tend to reproduce fragmented responsibility, externalised harm, procedural compliance, and short-term adaptation without deeper regeneration. Under pressure, ethical commitments become fragile when added as policy layers rather than embedded in the system’s foundational logic. Implications/Contributions: The paper contributes to discussions on viable and regenerative systems by proposing ontology as a practical design layer. It argues that sustainable governance requires coherence between what a system claims to preserve and what its underlying assumptions actually make possible. Ethical viability therefore depends on more coherent assumptions about interdependence, responsibility, and shared life.

Speaker: Jeremy Pryce (TBC) — Projekt Bergsjön

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Viability: A Way of Being
sessions.description:
John Beckford recalls Stafford Beer as a, very human, human being with the articulation of his arguments most easily understood through conversation. Beer’s evident care for humankind was expressed through the philosophy of ‘viability,’ a way of thinking rather than an alternative way of organising, a way of being rather than just a way of doing. The structural elements of Beer’s Viable System Model being a representation of activities necessary for survival rather than an alternative means of control, the pursuit of viability seeks to continuously dissolve the tension between any system, its metasystem and its environment.  Building on this insight leads to participatory approaches to developing the idea of viability with people and organisations especially through the development of shared mental models. Complementing this is the recognition that cybernetics is, in human organisations, about behaviour and ethics. Developing from this is Dudley's trialogue, a reformulation of the notion of the meta-system into a multi-partite conversation continuously resolving the tensions between current and future selves through clarity of identity and purpose.  If humankind is to thrive, cyberneticians need to consider more Beer’s philosophy of human well-being and less the puritanical and mechanistic adherence to a particular organisational form. Focusing on what the pursuit of viability means for human behaviour, liberty and interaction and being pragmatic in application will deliver much to a society being repressed by over-centralised governance and ultimately oppressive applications of technology. We must learn to pursue effectiveness and survival through the application and development of cybernetic ideas.  The style of this chapter is deliberately conversational – though the structure follows the key threads that the editors proposed could usefully be addressed. It consciously minimises the use of titles, sub-titles and connective tissue but is rigorously referenced to enable the interested reader to pursue the multiple threads of thought.

Speaker: John Beckford — Beckford Consulting

Room: Room B

sessions.title: Useful Art as a Toolkit for Cybernetic Change: A Viable Systems Model for a Better World Today
sessions.description:
This paper asks whether past utopias can serve as a portal for reimagining how today's high-powered technologies — AI, quantum computing, and beyond — might be redirected toward building a better world. Rather than one-size-fits-all, top-down, financialised solutions imposed by tech bros and populist leaders, it proposes a decentralised model rooted in real-world local innovation: linked micro-activisms empowered with ground-up capabilities, enabling dialogue to genuinely reach power. Central to this inquiry is the Cybersyn archive, approached as a site of latent potential for clarifying our present predicament. Drawing on Walter Benjamin's insistence that excavating past utopian dreams is a legitimate — even necessary — method for imagining alternatives, the paper revisits Stafford Beer's Viable System Model and the wider Cybersyn project as a resource for confronting today's complex technological landscape. A key comparative thread runs through the 1970s Latin American World Model (LAWM), developed in response to the Club of Rome's report that the world could not sustain its current trajectory. Where the Club of Rome saw limits, LAWM offered a qualified yes — if certain structural conditions were addressed. This paper argues that new global reports are, in effect, saying the same thing again, and that LAWM's logic remains instructive. Finally, the paper reactivates Marx's concept of the 'General Intellect' to theorise decentralised activist networks as fluid, self-regulating systems — and proposes Useful Art as the toolkit binding these local activisms into a coherent, networked, decentralised political economy. These are ideas which, in one form or another, I've been playing with for over twenty years, drawn together here as a proposal for thinking cybernetically about change, today.

Speaker: John Byrne — Liverpool John Moores University

Room: Room C

sessions.title: Towards new economic and social structures for a collaborative, post-capitalistic society
sessions.description:
The essence of Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM) is defined in his three books which had all been published by 1985. In the decades which have followed, the model has been applied and developed and inevitably has evolved to suit the environment in which it functions. Much of this - by Beer himself and many other consultants - has involved its successful application to traditional businesses in order to enhance the efficiency of the organisational structure and thus improve competiveness and profitability. In this Festschrift chapter, the original VSM will be re-examined, particularly the essence of Beer’s 5 VM Systems, and discussed to emphasise the ways in which the VSM presents a different and in many ways radical approach to the way we currently organise ourselves and opens the door to fundamental charges in the way we conduct ourselves in our daily lives, our businesses, and our governments. As the multiple crises which we face deepen, it become progressively more and more obvious that the issue of governance has to be addressed. Any successful way forward will require progress on multiple fronts and governance has to be a critically important part of the puzzle. This will require deep changes in the workings of a democratic state and the introduction of democracy into our businesses - which currently function in a similar way to a dictatorship. Many of Beer’s insights are of direct relevance to this debate – his laws and axioms all point in the same direction. At its core the VSM involves autonomous operational units interacting with their environment and the four Meta-systemic functions which provide the glue which ensures the operational units cohere into an effective totality. It will be argued that this inevitably leads to a structure which is not autocratic, requires individual creativity at the operational level and is based on collaboration. Clearly this is incompatible with both the Taylorist paradigm which dominated 20th Century views on organisation and still casts its shadow and the neo-liberal approach which focuses on minimal government intervention and ruthless competition. The chapter concludes with a speculative discussion of the kind of economic / political /social structures which Beer’s original model would suggest.

Speaker: Jon Walker — Metaphorum

Room: Room C

sessions.title: A full software implementation of Stafford Beer's Viable System Model (VSM) as a complete enterprise management system
sessions.description:
This talk presents a full software implementation of Stafford Beer's Viable System Model (VSM) as a complete enterprise management system, combining a live demonstration with a discussion of the system's capabilities, the methodologies behind it, and the challenges encountered during development. The system is a stand-alone desktop application supporting multiple, freely extensible levels of recursion, with real-time connections to the environment via configurable feeds. It manages a wide range of organisational functions: recursion analysis, process management, task coordination, output control, vertical coherence analysis, and audit of key variables. Connections between the environment and internal systems — and between internal systems themselves — are managed through homeostats built from transductors that use Bayesian decision mechanisms to switch the governing states of processes defining key properties. Where this falls short of covering the full variety of situations, a Pask conversation mechanism is provided to support semantic transduction across boundaries. The system also operates in a manner comparable to project management, but purpose-built for the VSM. It enables resources with defined work patterns and properties to be assigned tasks, goals, and objectives to achieve specific outputs. This supports resource allocation across manpower, materials, information, and ideas. The system is capable of HR management; stock control; financial costing and analysis; monitoring organisational integrity and viability — including simulation of the organisation's operations through forward time projection, and Monte Carlo sweeps across key variables to monitor viability. The talk concludes with a discussion of the future roadmap: evolving the system from a desktop application into a distributed system supporting multiple concurrent users and networked deployment across an organisation. A further direction under consideration is a blockchain-based consensus mechanism to support cooperative, multi-stakeholder decision-making — of particular relevance to organisations such as cooperatives, where authority is distributed rather than centralised.

Speaker: Captain Jonathan Huxley

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Architecture for Freedom: Syntegrity as an Educational Practice
sessions.description:
Purpose: Stafford Beer taught us that a structure, by setting its own limits and constraints, can open rather than close possibilities. Architectural education, we think, should mirror a cybernetic architecture: a structured framework that, by setting limits and constraints, creates space for freedom, a freedom that emerges through dialogue with the unknown, through the encounter with the other. Following Beer's Designing Freedom, we call this an architecture for freedom.  Methods: We built a design course inspired by Beer's Team Syntegrity, letting it take several shapes across a few years. First, only among students, working through readings in rotating roles of advocate, critic and observer, so a shared understanding could grow without us dictating it. Then the syntegrations opened outward, putting students in dialogue with a village theatre group, inside that same non-hierarchical structure. Later, we stepped back, and the students designed and ran their own syntegration involving the community.  Findings: In this process with the students, the structure did the teaching more than we did. Students moved from solving problems previously framed to designing the very process of designing, in Chris Jones's sense, building up a confidence to approach others they did not yet know, just as the structure had once engaged them. Implications: This is what an architecture for freedom looks like in a classroom: cybernetics mirroring the long-standing tradition of architecture, offering a framework that encompasses the symbolic, the bodily, the intellectual and the concrete, and like Beer's icosahedron, holds just enough space for people to find their own way through it.

Speaker: Jose S. Cabral Filho — Federal University of Minas Gerais (Brazil)

Room: Room D

sessions.title: A Cybernetic Architecture for AI Governance: Integrating Identity, VSM, and Organizational Pathologies
sessions.description:
This Festschrift chapter presents an organizational cybernetic approach that integrates the Viable System Model (VSM) with the Taxonomy of Organizational Pathologies (TOP) to address contemporary complexity and the diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI). It begins by positing “identity” as an essential dimension, alongside anatomy, physiology, and neurology, and requires analysts to adopt an external vantage point to clarify who the organization is, why it exists, and where its boundaries lie. From this identity-centred stance, environmental and organizational complexity are unfolded into recursion levels, guided by Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety and structured through the Recursion Levels–Key Factors Matrix, enabling a coherent “multi-universe” cartography of PAN-VSM configurations. On this basis, the chapter describes a top down, four stage framework: clarification of identity, purpose, and boundaries; construction of the vertical recursive structure; diagnosis or design of each organization–environment pair using VSM components (Systems 1–5 and communication channels); and a coherence check across levels. This architecture directly addresses criticisms that VSM is static, outdated, or excessively objective by embedding dynamics through System 4, scenario modelling, and explicitly incorporating stakeholder perceptions through protocols for surfacing and integrating subjective views. TOP complements the framework with a controlled vocabulary of structural, functional, and information/communication pathologies that reveal flaws in recursion design, in the balance of Systems 1–5, and in critical channels and signals. In the context of AI diffusion, the combined VSM–TOP lens illuminates systemic risks such as (for example): ill-defined identities guiding AI strategies, institutional schizophrenia in conflicting AI policies, autopoietic “beasts” overpowering metasystems, or missing or distorted channels that amplify misinformation.

Speaker: Jose Manuel Perez Rios — University of Valladolid, Spain

Room: Room B

sessions.title: Transparency as a Trigger for Change: Repercussions of the Viable System Model (VSM) Application on Water Governance in the Tocantins-Araguaia Hydrographic Region
sessions.description:
Purpose: This study examines the repercussions of applying Stafford Beer's Viable System Model (VSM) as a diagnostic and design tool for water governance in two River Basin Organizations (RBOs) within the Tocantins-Araguaia Hydrographic Region, Brazil, as part of the Cyber-Rivers Project. The analysis focuses on how the structural transparency produced by the VSM influenced concrete institutional change. The target audience comprises professionals interested in a systemic-cybernetic approach to management and organization. Methods: The case study methodology was chosen, which enables long-term, insightful investigations. The case covers the trajectory from the structural diagnostic of the two hydric systems, over the decisions to implement organizational change, until their repercussions within four to five years. For the analysis and diagnosis of structures, we revert to Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model. Our notation for referencing the components of the model follows established convention: The regulatory systems are labeled S1 … S5. Findings: By exposing latent structural deficits - fragmented operational units (S1), weak coordination (S2), limited monitoring (S3*), disconnection between executive management and strategic intelligence (S3-S4), and a passive normative function (S5) - the VSM diagnosis catalyzed measurable institutional responses. Investment in water policy instruments increased from R$40,000 to R$1 million, and a River Basin Agency was created to address the operational and coordination gaps identified. This way dramatic deficits of both the functioning and the management of the hydric systems under study were overcome. Implications: These outcomes suggest that the VSM's contribution extended beyond prescriptive recommendations, functioning as an epistemic device that rendered the system observable to itself. By restoring recursive integrity, strengthening operational autonomy, and unblocking homeostatic feedback mechanisms, the model created the cognitive and political conditions for stakeholders to mobilize structural reform, offering a replicable pathway for cybernetic diagnosis to inform water governance elsewhere.

Speaker: Juliana Mariano Alves — Universidade Estadual do Tocantins

Room: Room C

sessions.title: The Speed Gap — Translating the Viable System Model for a New Generation of Practitioners
sessions.description:
A century after Stafford Beer's birth, the problem he named has not gone away; it has intensified. Organisations face a faster, AI-saturated, more distributed environment in which the management of variety is now experienced, day to day, as a shortage of time. Yet much of the practitioner field that wrestles with this problem does so without naming the VSM. Managers reach for adjacent idioms — agile, platforms, machine learning — that regulate variety without the conceptual rigour Beer gave us. The relevance of the VSM is growing; its citation is not keeping pace. This session takes that gap seriously and asks a demand-side question: not “what becomes of Beer?” but “what must an organisation become, and where does cybernetics earn its place?” It introduces The Tautai Principle (Mathis, 2025) not as a rival framework but as one practitioner translation of the VSM — a vocabulary built for managers who never say “System 1,” yet who are solving System-1-to-System-5 problems every week. The talk does three things. First, it restates the contemporary challenge as requisite variety felt as response latency — the “speed gap” — and shows why this framing reaches audiences that “variety” alone does not. Second, it offers a transparent correspondence map between the Tautai vocabulary (the three gaps, the four capabilities, navigation-versus-planning, identity-as-asset, the organisational nervous system) and the constructs of the VSM (Ashby's Law, the S3–S4 homeostat, variety engineering, S5 identity, S2 and algedonic channels). Each correspondence is judged honestly on a single axis: does the practitioner framing carry the cybernetic content faithfully, extend it where Beer's model was under-specified (cadence, decisionability under AI, the politics of transition), or lose something essential (recursion, the homeostat, falsifiability)? Third, it draws the consequence for this community. A published framework that re-derives viability, distributed regulation and identity without Beer's name is a live instance of the scenario in which “the principles win and the name becomes optional.” That is not a threat to the VSM but evidence of its reach — and an on-ramp for non-Beerian practitioners into the deeper model. The session closes with the deflationary counter-argument considered squarely: if speed-talk merely re-skins cybernetics, what, if anything, has been gained? The aim is constructive: to show that the VSM's role is growing precisely because the problem is growing, and that faithful translation is one of the ways a hundred-year-old model keeps earning its place.

Speaker: Krishan Mathis

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Cybernetic Futures (workshop)
sessions.description:
A hundred years after Stafford Beer's birth, this workshop asks what the next hundred years of organizational cybernetics could look like — and what we should do now to shape them. Rather than a retrospective, Cybernetic Futuresis a working session: participants explore plausible development trajectories and derive concrete options for intervention, with particular attention to strengthening democratic structures and the agency of individuals and groups to shape the future. We distinguish five horizons of 'future' relevant to cybernetics: the future of Beer's specific models (notably the Viable System Model), of cybernetic principles more broadly, of organizations, of AI and machine intelligence, and of society itself. The specific artifacts may change, while the underlying principles may become more relevant rather than less. From a set of scenarios — for example AI Revives Cybernetics, Cybernetics Merges with Complexity Science, The Rise of Collective Sensemaking Systems, and Planetary Cybernetics — we run a selection in parallel as starting points for structured discussion. The format is a syntegration-inspired discovery lab combining short provocations, structured small-group dialogue with rotating roles and timeboxing, and collective synthesis — not presentation-only. Each group documents its work as raw material for subsequent analysis. Senior figures take the role of respondents and witnesses; younger and practitioner voices contribute on equal footing. Outputs feed a continuing 'group for the future' and a publication trail beyond the conference. Participants leave with a shared set of questions worth pursuing and a concrete sense of where cybernetic practice can intervene.

Speaker: Krishan Mathis

Room: Room B

sessions.title: The Social Movement of Tomorrow: Sharing Practical VSM Application
sessions.description:
'An Organization is What it Does'; this is the lesson of the Viable System Model (VSM) that resonated with me the most strongly. However, for environmental movements, civil society organizations, and cooperatives – types of volunteer organizations which I have also taken part in – a big disconnect exists between sustainable, decolonial, or inclusive aims and lived practice: Common problematic patterns are contested identity, an unsustainable reliance on a select group of members, a lack of foresight about the organizational environment, and a decreased ability to measure the organization's health. Contemporary applications of the VSM have shown its usefulness as a framework to remedy these problems. However, they are often expert-led and target highly institutional groups such as businesses and governments. As a vector to propagate social change, grassroots organizations are critical to transition to global viable and sustainable praxis. However, there are many challenges in applying the VSM in grassroots contexts. Among them are its high complexity, high strategical requirements for scalability and accessibility, suspicion towards centralized technological infrastructure, and inherent tensions between data collection vs. privacy as well as transparency vs. secrecy. In this session, I will share a method for participatory self-transformation adapted to this context and shaped through fieldwork. As a starting point, print materials and software employed in my work with individuals and organizations will be presented to familiarize participants with current activities and their challenges and opportunities. Finally, participants are invited to ask questions about design choices and share their own views and experiences.

Speaker: Leon Bellin — Copernicus Institute

Room: Room C

sessions.title: Measuring Organizational Viability Beyond Structure: The CO4 and Biovariety Framework
sessions.description:
Purpose: The Viable System Model (VSM) has demonstrated strong explanatory and practical value across diverse organizational contexts. However, organizations may preserve the formal architecture of viability while losing the relational conditions that sustain adaptation. This paper introduces the CO4–Biovariety framework as a relational extension of the VSM, proposing that viability depends on functional differentiation and the continuous conservation of relational organization. Methods: Grounded in Relational Trifferential Logic, the framework integrates two developments. CO4 evaluates viability through four relational dimensions—Cohesion, Communication, Coordination, and Conduct—while Biovariety assesses relational continuity by distinguishing required from non-required variety. Together, they provide operational indicators of functional hypertrophy, relational degradation, and declining adaptive capacity before structural deterioration becomes evident. Findings: Applications in mining, public healthcare, higher education, and public administration show that organizations with similar functional architectures can differ substantially in relational viability. The framework identifies cases in which increasing functional complexity consumes relational resources, reducing adaptive capacity despite preserving structural coherence. Implications/Contributions: The framework extends organizational cybernetics by complementing structural assessment with measures of relational organization. It provides a practical diagnostic methodology for earlier detection of organizational deterioration and measurable indicators supporting intervention, organizational learning, and adaptive governance. The paper argues that sustainable organizational viability is fundamentally a relational property rather than solely a structural one.

Speaker: Leonardo Lavanderos (TBC)

Room: Room C

sessions.title: Beer’s Pedagogy: Lessons from the Concordia University Lectures
sessions.description:
Stafford Beer’s writings have been widely recognized as novel, erudite, profound and influential, shaping decades of contributions from scholars and practitioners alike. They have also been criticized as opaque and difficult to apply, contributing to a tendency for his work to exist on the margins of mainstream academia and management. Beer was sensitive to these critiques. By his own account, he penned Diagnosing the System in part to address these concerns. In it, he provides a step-by-step stripped-down approach to understanding and deploying the viable systems model (VSM) for managers and others interested in how the analytical tool could help with real-world decision-making. In the forward to Diagnosing the System, Beer says the book was inspired and shaped by his experienced co-teaching the VSM in a seminar course offered at Concordia, Montreal, Canada, in 1981-82.  He devotes the book to the students of this class, insisting that the book resulted from “my learning.” My contribution will share reflections on what we can learn from Stafford Beer’s approach to pedagogy by analyzing recently digitalized recordings of these lectures.  My method is interpretative and is inspired by a second-order cybernetics perspective of a ‘model of the modeler,’ paying close attention to Beer’s pedagogical approach and indications of self-awareness about his pedagogical style. I expect that this analysis will help us understand how we might learn from Beer’s pedagogy and better communicate and teach about the VSM. It will also shed some light on Beer’s time in Canada, a place he would eventually call home until his passing in 2002 and which figured prominently in Diagnosing the System and in other of his later works.

Speaker: Marc-André Pigeon — Canadian Centre for the Study of Co-operatives

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Enactive Viable Agency: A Process Relational Grammar for Meta-Cybernetics and the VSM
sessions.description:
Contemporary social, ecological, and organizational crises increasingly reveal failures of collective agency rather than simply failures of governance. The Viable System Model (VSM) offers one of the most powerful cybernetic frameworks for understanding organizational viability, yet its functional architecture can be difficult to interpret and operationalize without oversimplification or misapplication. This work describes the relational processes implicit within and between the subsystems of the VSM, using a process-relational grammar that renders its recursive architecture interpretable and operational across multiple domains. Drawing on Enactive Cognitive Science, the proposed grammar interprets viability through recursively organized relational processes, offering an alternative to command-and-control or purely informational interpretations of the VSM. Moreover, this emphasis reveals the structural correspondences among the VSM, the Noble Eightfold Path, and Meta-Cybernetics. This integration forms a recursive model of agency I refer to as the Enactive Viable Agency (EVA) model, which emerged through a comparative metatheoretical analysis of these models.
