The VSM primarily describes the recursive organization of viable systems, whereas EVA describes the reflexive dynamics through which viable agency interprets, reorganizes, and transforms itself. Applied diagnostically, EVA highlights how fragmentation of agency contributes to failures of coordination across individual, organizational, and societal systems. It provides a diagnostic framework for identifying the types of relationships needed to foster viability, with implications for the design of techno-cultural systems that augment collective agency. Thus, EVA provides an accessible, structured language that operationalizes a functional architecture of recursive agency.

Speaker: Marcus Barrick

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Organizational Cybernetics in the Age of AI: Toward an Epistemic Conception of Viability
sessions.description:
Purpose: Organizational cybernetics has traditionally defined viability in functional terms, emphasizing survival, adaptation, and complexity management. However, the growing reliance on generative AI and digital decision-support systems exposes the limitations of this perspective by highlighting the epistemic processes through which organizations construct and interpret reality. This paper proposes an epistemic conception of viability that integrates constructivist epistemology and second-order cybernetics. Methods: The study adopts a conceptual and theoretical methodology, critically examining classical and second-order organizational cybernetics alongside constructivist epistemology. It first analyses the tension between constructivist assumptions and prevailing functional interpretations of viability, then investigates how AI intensifies epistemic vulnerabilities. Building on this analysis, the paper develops an epistemic framework of organizational viability and proposes a knowledge governance model grounded in selective attention, interpretive flexibility, reflexivity, and plurality. Findings: The paper argues that organizational viability depends not only on functional adaptation but also on the capacity to generate, critically evaluate, and revise organizational knowledge. AI increases informational capacity while potentially reinforcing epistemic fragility through algorithmic opacity, interpretive homogenization, and overreliance on automated outputs. An epistemic conception of viability therefore requires organizations to preserve interpretive diversity, reflexive learning, and responsible knowledge governance.

Speaker: Maria Giovanna Corrado

Room: Room A

sessions.title: CyberSystemic Tools for Organizational Advancement
sessions.description:
CyberSystemic Tools for Organizational Advancement, by Markus Schwaninger.  The approach outlined in this chapter helps to enhance the connectivity and synergy of exponents from different fields: Their capabilities are fused in joint efforts towards organizational advancement – not just in economic terms but in a much broader sense. This is a conceptual-theoretical contribution. First, the concept of Management is explored from a cybersystemic stance. Second, Systemic Management is analyzed as a key to Organizational Intelligence. To bind these components together, an integrative Framework for the Design and Development of Intelligent Organizations is proposed. This framework has five dimensions rooted in the research tradition of systemic management: Activities, Structure, Behavior, Basic Parameters, Time. For each one of these dimensions cybersystemic tools are proposed. The presented concept is applicable to organizations of all kinds, but also to societies at large, to social initiatives and movements. The study is an effort to open paths to a new organizational paradigm: one that transcends the technocratic, unidimensional, reductionist approaches to management. The quest is for viability and development, - making possible humane organizations and a sustainable future that is worth living for.

Speaker: Markus Schwaninger — University of St. Gallen, Switzerland

Room: Room B

sessions.title: From Theory to Practice – and Back
sessions.description:
I have dedicated my professional mission to the practical application of Stafford’s models and methods. I now have 30 years of experience applying Syntegration, the VSM and Operations Rooms in all kinds of organisations – large and small, business and non-business. In my presentation, I would like to share what I have learned from more than 300 Syntegrations, close to 100 VSM consulting projects, and training over 1000 executives in the VSM – across Europe, the Americas and Asia. I will highlight some key success factors I have identified in practice and relate them back to the underlying theory.

Speaker: Martin Pfiffner

Room: Room B

sessions.title: From Cybersyn to the City: Variety Engineering and the Design of Open Urban Infrastructures
sessions.description:
Contemporary urban digital twins (UDTs) are frequently deployed as tools of technocratic optimization, reducing cities to data mirrors that serve efficiency rather than democratic participation. This paper argues that Stafford Beer's cybernetic principles, particularly variety engineering (Beer, 1979, 1993), offer a rigorous alternative for designing UDTs as instruments of citizen empowerment rather than centralized control. Building on a framework for participatory UDTs grounded in Beer's Viable System Model and lessons from Project Cybersyn (Medina, 2011), this paper expands the treatment of variety engineering by distinguishing eigen-variety, the internal capacity of citizens and institutions to act, from hetero-variety, the complexity of the urban environment (Schwaninger & Ott, 2023). Drawing on Ashby's law of requisite variety (Ashby, 1956) and its recent formalization (Schwaninger & Ott, 2023), we show how amplification and attenuation function as complementary levers: attenuation renders overwhelming urban complexity legible without flattening it into a technocratic dashboard, while amplification expands citizens' capacity to engage meaningfully with governance. The paper then points to a digital twin platform currently under development that operationalizes these principles through federated, interoperable data structures and algedonic feedback mechanisms (Beer, 1981), in contrast to the vertical, single-point decision structures typical of commercial smart city platforms. Rather than concentrating variety management in one technical layer, the tool distributes it across autonomous subsystems tied to different stakeholders, echoing Cybersyn's recursive architecture (Medina, 2011) while addressing its historical shortcomings in decentralization. Positioned within the theme of Emerging Methods and Tools, this contribution argues that Beer's project remains extremely relevant in face of the new developments of digital platforms and offers the conceptual tools for building open, participatory information infrastructures suited to governing complex urban and social systems.

Speaker: Mateus van Stralen — Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG)

Room: Room C

sessions.title: Charting the Boundaries of Accountability for Enhanced Airport Operational Resilience
sessions.description:
Busy commercial airports are very ‘large’ intricate systems where up to several hundred organisations keep ‘stepping onto one another’s toes’, to the detriment of the operational effectiveness, resilience and viability of the whole. Boundaries of accountability are poorly understood. Over three decades of liberalisation of global air transport has created situations of largely decentralised control, where behaviours of least use to the collectivity (passengers included) are incentivised, and effective steersmanship is hindered. Mandated by the UK’s Civil Aviation Authority to urgently enhance its on-time performance, a major UK airport operator embarked with the University of Edinburgh on a quest for a new experimental epistemology of airport operational resilience. In particular, we sought one that incentivises effective dynamic interactions across its (eco)system of airport stakeholders. Applying the VSM, we developed and tested a new toolbox of audits (System 3*) to enhance the airport’s capacity to absorb variety. Highlights include (i) cyber-systemic means to find out where the accountability boundaries actually lie and (ii) an implementation of Beer’s indices of performance that, measuring across any one such boundary, highlights promising routes for effective intervention. All the tools employ existing airport data feeds and are now regularly used by the airport operator to facilitate meaningful cross-organisational problem-solving. Validation at two other European airports took place. Following that, we were invited to partake in EUROCONTROL’s current work aimed at harmonizing airport performance measurement across Europe. We conclude the paper by discussing the extent to which our contributions are applicable to non-airport contexts.

Speaker: Maurizio Tomasella — University of Edinburgh Business School

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Design of a Cybernetic Governance Framework for Platform Tokenomics
sessions.description:
Two-sided market platforms in their early stages must coordinate buyers and sellers whilst remaining adaptable as they develop a viable dynamic organisational structure. This paper addresses such a challenge, through a programme of action research. We engage with a realworld, blockchain-enabled platform start-up whose founder aims to create in the long-term a democratised form of decentralised autonomous organisation (DAO). Decentralisation is not treated as an immediate condition to be met at the outset, but instead as a strategic idealised endpoint that can only be approached indefinitely once the platform has had the opportunity to develope the requisite coordination, control, and adaptability mechanisms needed to sustain it.  We use the Viable System Model (VSM) as the framework to unpack the dynamic mechanisms fostering the underpinning transition. We develop representative conceptual models of such mechanisms and then translate them into formal models amenable to scientific analysis. Through extensive simulations, we then derive more general conditions for similar platforms to successfully pass the test of time and reach long-term viability. The paper offers a pragmatic account of platform design, especially the role of token tradability and its implications for long-term platform viability supported by tokens granting governance rights. We conclude that genuine decentralisation in tokenised DAOs is more likely to emerge from a centralised viable organisation through successive relaxations on the central vertical axis, rather than by attempts to impose decentralisation at launch, this view is consistent with the known idea that “the purpose of a system is what it does” (POSIWID).

Speaker: Miguel Garcia Matas — University of Edinburgh

Room: Room C

sessions.title: Elevating Stafford Beer’s Legacy: A Critical Systems Thinking Perspective on the Viable System Model
sessions.description:
The importance of Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM) is increasingly recognised. For this to continue, and his legacy to be enhanced, it is necessary to understand the assumptions on which the VSM is based, how the model relates to other significant contributions to systems thinking and practice, and what it can achieve. This keynote argues that Critical Systems Thinking (CST) is well placed to assist in these matters. CST embraces the philosophy of pragmatism and views the VSM as part of that tradition. It is not, on this reading, a scientific model or a ‘hermeneutic enabler’. It is useful because it has demonstrated what Dewey calls ‘warranted assertibility’. This conclusion has significant methodological implications. CST seeks to provide a critique of systems approaches based on the ‘systemic perspectives’ they privilege. On this criterion, the VSM shares an organismic orientation with socio-technical systems thinking, contingency theory, and the many contemporary descriptions of organisations as ‘living systems’. There is much to learn from these other organismic accounts although the explanatory power provided by cybernetics puts the VSM in pole position for unifying their findings and guiding the action research necessary to further develop the power of this perspective. CST argues that it is necessary to be multi-perspectival and multi-methodological in the face of real-world complexity. Clarity around the theoretical underpinnings of the VSM enables us to understand better its relationship to alternative systems approaches privileging mechanical, interrelationships, purposeful, and societal/environmental perspectives. The way forward is not to ‘expand’ the VSM (threatening its integrity), or to ‘mix’ approaches (threatening cognitive loss) to achieve ‘greater coverage’ of the various ways in which complexity announces itself, but to continue to enhance its distinct competences and become adept at using it in combination with other systems approaches in pursuit of multi-dimensional improvement. CST offers valuable insights, I believe, into how best to view and use the VSM, thus opening a clear pathway for those seeking to elevate Stafford Beer’s legacy.

Speaker: Michael C. Jackson — University of Hull, UK

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Can Stafford Beer Help Save Journalism? Applying the Viable System Model to Understand Resilience in Public Service Media
sessions.description:
News organisations face growing complexity from artificial intelligence, misinformation, fragmented audiences and declining public trust. Journalism is one of society’s primary sensemaking systems, helping citizens interpret complexity and make informed decisions. Yet systems thinking is rarely applied to understanding news organisations themselves. This paper explores how Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM), integrated with Soft Systems Methodology (SSM) and Critical Systems Heuristics (CSH), can strengthen organisational resilience within an anonymised public service media organisation. Methods: An anonymised organisational case study was undertaken using a mixed-methods systems inquiry. Semi-structured interviews, workshops, documentary analysis and systems mapping informed the application of VSM to examine organisational viability, SSM to surface multiple stakeholder worldviews, and CSH to critically examine boundary judgements, assumptions and whose perspectives shaped organisational decision-making.  Findings: The study found that the principal barriers to organisational effectiveness were systemic rather than technological. Fragmented ownership, weak feedback loops and competing stakeholder perspectives constrained organisational learning and adaptive capacity. Integrating VSM, SSM and CSH produced a richer organisational diagnosis than any single methodology alone. The findings further suggest that diversity should be understood not only as an ethical objective but also as a cybernetic capability. Drawing on Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety, the study argues that diversity constitutes a source of requisite variety, increasing an organisation’s capacity to perceive, interpret and respond effectively to environmental complexity.  Implications/Contributions: The paper proposes an integrated systems framework for diagnosing organisational complexity and strengthening organisational viability in public service media. It demonstrates the contemporary relevance of Stafford Beer’s cybernetic principles and argues that resilient organisations require not only effective structures but also sufficient diversity of perspectives, critical reflection and continuous learning. In doing so, it illustrates how Beer’s ideas continue to offer practical guidance for designing resilient and ethical organisations beyond their traditional domains. More broadly, it argues that if journalism is to help society make sense of complexity, news organisations must themselves become systems-literate.

Speaker: Nour Abida

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Bridging PIMS Data and Cybernetics: An Externally Anchored Operations Room
sessions.description:
Purpose: Management cybernetics and empirical strategy data grew up as separate traditions. This session bridges them: it introduces the PIMS programme — six decades of confidential cross-industry data on some 4,300 business units — and Beer’s Viable System Model, then builds a quantitative version of his operations room for the individual business unit. Methods: Beer’s triple index — Actuality, Capability, Potentiality — is measured not on profit alone but across the essential variables that determine a business’s viability, each judged against ranges drawn from evidence rather than negotiated targets. The distinctive step is where the reference points come from: Capability and Potentiality are set not from inside the system, as in Cybersyn, but externally, by comparing a business with the peers in the data that most closely resemble it. Findings. External reference points reveal underperformance against a unit’s own demonstrated potential that internal, negotiable targets tend to hide, and surface warning signs — in market position or innovation — long before they reach the accounts. Where data allows, a limited business-unit example will illustrate the environment in use. Implications: The result is a repeatable format that gives the strategic level of an organisation — Beer’s System 3–4 — an external evidence base to match its internal actuals, while leaving variable selection, interpretation and judgement with the organisation itself. The essential variables and their ranges must be rebuilt for each domain; the triple index and the underlying discipline transfer directly.

Speaker: Louis Harel — pims.ai | malik

Room: Room B

sessions.title: Designing Viable Identity in Institutional Transitions: A VSM Reconstruction of the Total Veteran Framework
sessions.description:
Purpose: This article reconstructs Total Veteran through the Viable System Model (VSM) to develop the Viable Identity Adaptation Framework (VIAF), a conceptual model for understanding and designing identity adaptation during major institutional transitions. It argues that post-military reintegration should not be reduced to employability, entrepreneurship training or psychological adjustment, but understood as the systemic redesign of viable identity, self-environment models, regulatory capacity, coordination and renewed domains of action. Design/methodology/approach: The article offers a theoretically informed reconstruction of Total Veteran as a case of transition from a highly structured military environment into civilian and entrepreneurial life. It uses the VSM as an analytical and design architecture to reinterpret the functions embedded in Total Veteran and to abstract a transferable framework for organizational and cultural change. The argument draws on organizational cybernetics, organizational identity, sensemaking, second-order learning and second-order cybernetics. Findings: The reconstruction suggests that viable identity adaptation depends on the interaction of six functions: identity and purpose formation, self-environment model reconstruction, regulatory translation, monitoring and early-warning feedback, coordination among operational domains, and operational experimentation in renewed domains of autonomy. Controlled, incremental exposure to new environments emerges as catalytic because it allows identity coherence to be tested, self-environment models to be revised, regulatory needs to surface and new agency to be enacted. Originality/value: The article extends the VSM from organizational diagnosis toward the design of viable identity adaptation in institutional transitions. It positions Total Veteran as a generative case for VIAF and offers a design logic for veteran reintegration, organizational change, cultural transformation and VSM-based systemic practice.

Speaker: Pedro Pablo Cardoso — University of Exeter / De Montfort University

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Insufficient Variety and Artificial Intelligence
sessions.description:
In my interactions with Stafford before he died, he was constantly making apparent that he was searching for a better world, but at the same time he was deeply aware that ongoing human processes were not supporting this outcome. Perhaps efforts towards a less chaotic and better managed complex world could help overcoming these limitations. Cybernetic methodological contributions could be platforms for the effective management of policy issues. This is what I want to offer in these conversations from the perspective of WOSC. More transformations of environmental inputs into necessary economic outputs, may help seeing the world as ecological systems, reducing instances of failure and increasing examples of good performance.  Attention to interactions, relationships and complexity are contributions to increasing the possibilities to make things happen in a chaotic world. People need to deal with shared concerns, more specifically they need to work with shared policies in chaotic situations of high complexity. Disagreements and collaboration require their shared attention. It is in these contexts that managing complexity is a challenge. Ross Ashby offers in his book “An Introduction to Cybernetics” (1964) the Law of Requisite Variety, but it is in Stafford Beer’s book “Designing Freedom” (1972), that a great and most useful contribution to this law is given to society and management. Following this, in my early work with Nigel Howard (Espejo and Howard, 1982) we highlighted the “Law of Insuficient Variety”, which I elaborate in my methodological work (Espejo, 2025). My emphasis now is on poiesis to produce desirable worlds, in the context of enframing them in cyber-systemic models. From a cybernetic perspective I expect a focus on correcting variety imbalances among the myriad of relationships producing our world. Thus, this is an invitation, following Stafford’s work to use the law of requisite variety in the world we are producing over time. We are aware that First and Second Order Cybernetics could be powerful contributions towards better societies in a complex world. In our view the complexity of policy issues has ontological and epistemological underpinnings that cybernetics and systems may help to structure better. Adequate relationships and resources may help people and groups to develop better structures. These are structures to produce better policy issues, underpinning social issues through language and related meanings. Stronger organisational structures are necessary for more ethical and cohesive elaboration of policy issues. This is a challenge for Artificial Intelligence.

Speaker: Raúl Espejo — World Organization of Systems and Cybernetics

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Cybersyn Boxes. Prototyping a Document Visualisation Assisted by AI
sessions.description:
The Cybersyn Project records in the Stafford Beer Archive (SBA) at Liverpool John Moores University offer insight into cybernetic and management science thought, capturing the intellectual process behind concepts like the Viable System Model (VSM) through handwritten notes, diagrams, and correspondence. Currently, there is no visualisation that supports relational exploration of these archives, making it difficult to trace how ideas, correspondence, and diagrams connect. Data visualisation is a way to show complex structures visually, facilitating pattern recognition and exploration. This project argues for representing collections like the SBA through visualisation, enabling multi-perspective views of records and going beyond the usual document-by-document viewing. The project explores visualisation to support navigation through these documents, revealing how individual records relate to the whole and how people and concepts connect, and enabling intuitive exploration of complex archives. This project addresses three challenges: (a) adapting knowledge graphs to the archival materials, (b) developing strategies for natural-language querying, and (c) designing automated visualisation. In doing so, it advances research in Visualisation, Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), and Digital Humanities by treating visualisation as a means of knowledge discovery. Building on this, the project clarifies how GenAI, LLMs, and Knowledge Graphs enhance visualisation, opening access to an archive significant to the history of technology in Chile and the world. This proposal seeks to show some of the project's progress, allowing an overview of the potential applications across different areas such as human rights, arts, and the humanities, among others.

Speaker: Ricardo Vega Mora — Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile (PUC)

Room: Room B

sessions.title: From Evidence to Inquiry: Keeping LLM Inference Provisional in Recursive VSM Diagnosis
sessions.description:
Purpose: Clemson’s VSM ToolBox and Pérez Ríos’s VSMod showed how software can support Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM); LLMs introduce a different cybernetic problem: plausible inference can harden into organisational fact and propagate across recursion levels. This project builds a traceable path from evidence to hypotheses, questions and candidate interventions. Methods: The prototype was applied to two public-record cases: Robin Hood Energy and the Charity Commission inquiry into New Wineskins Charitable Trust and U-Turn Move on Homes. It proposes operations, relations and recursive structure, promoting each only when an evidence-gated test passes; otherwise it abstains. Structural gaps become an agenda of focused questions; answers and corrections persist through reanalysis. Testable structural hypotheses and candidate prescriptions each carry a check that could confirm or refute them. When an LLM-attributed record includes a quotation and citations, the quotation must match the cited source text verbatim. Findings: Both demonstrations produced evidence-linked maps, diagnostic observations and explicit gaps. In one, an entered answer that no role monitored the external environment or future was retained verbatim as evidence of a System 4 gap; no function was invented to fill it. VSM operates as a reasoning grammar, not only a diagram. Implications/Contributions: The contribution is a persistent evidence-to-inquiry loop that turns abstention into diagnostic work while model suggestions remain provisional. Results demonstrate software traceability, not diagnostic validity or organisational impact. Practitioner testing comes next. When should AI-proposed structure become a diagnostic premise?

Speaker: Richard Gunther — Recursive Systems

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Cybernetics of Community Development – A TEAM (Thinking with Every Available Mind) Activity
sessions.description:
My contributions to establishing the Bloomfield Community Centre in Narberth, Pembrokeshire (1980s), and founding the Todmorden Learning Centre in West Yorkshire (2010s) have led to the understanding presented here.  The two central themes of community development:- providing opportunities for establishing and developing relationships between members of the community; understanding successful democratic cooperative managing of the processes involved; viz- Creating a community hub where members of the community can meet so that new relationships are made and old relationships are strengthened. The hub must be welcoming to all, drawing people in to enjoy themselves, discuss problems, and begin the tasks of improving the community. The hub should become a seeding ground for ideas, and collective help, establishing community enterprises which are grounded in supporting the community and in cooperative ideals. This will lessen dependence on outside provision of the necessary goods and services that are required by the community. Ensuring the ideals and culture developed in the hub become those of the formal community government will further enable development towards sustainability, opening the possibility of new funding. Spreading the ideas and culture of sustainability and cooperation to surrounding communities, helping build their communities toward sustainability will strengthen our community in trading locally, gathering new ideas, and helping others. Working together with neighbouring communities when they have achieved the first four stages of this journey will enable this culture and way of being to move to the next level of governing.

Speaker: Robin Asby

Room: Room C

sessions.title: Foundations in Dialogue: Comparing VSM and CSH through Checkland’s FMA Framework
sessions.description:
Purpose: Metaphorum 2026 marks Stafford Beer’s centenary and, following Peter Checkland’s passing, offers an opportunity to revisit the foundations of systems practice. This paper compares Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM) with the critical systems tradition developed from C. West Churchman through Werner Ulrich’s Critical Systems Heuristics (CSH), including its critical-realist extension, CSH 2.0. Methods: Using Checkland and Holwell’s FMA framework, we distinguish the frameworks of ideas (F) underpinning each approach, the methodological resources through which they are enacted (M), and their use in a shared organisational area of concern (A). The inquiry is conducted as an asymmetric dialogue between a CSH specialist and a methodologically pluralist practitioner experienced in Soft Systems Methodology, system dynamics and VSM. Kuhn informs our treatment of theory-laden terminology and the risks of translation across paradigmatic traditions. We compare ontological, epistemological and axiological assumptions; criteria of adequate inquiry; and differing treatments of purpose, boundary, control, variety, complexity and the affected. Findings: We argue that VSM and CSH are neither substitutes nor directly commensurable methodologies. VSM primarily examines the organisational and regulatory conditions for viability, whereas CSH critically examines the boundary judgements, knowledge claims, interests and legitimacy of proposed improvements. Through an illustrative application and reciprocal critique, we identify where the approaches converge, complement one another, remain non-equivalent or stand in tension. Implications/Contributions: The contribution is practical guidance for selecting and relating the approaches, together with an iterative boundary–viability inquiry intended to generate reframings and interventions not produced by either initial analysis alone.

Speaker: Roelien Goede — North-West University, South Africa

Room: Room A

sessions.title: Artificial intelligence as a liberty machine. A metamodelization of barefoot cybernetics
sessions.description:
Stafford Beer invented a metasystemic language to produce liberty machines of competent information, with which we could empower human freedom. Good old fashioned artificial intelligence (GOFAI) models are articulated to the hierarchical organizations, dominated by the signifiers of money and the white, wise, colonizer, patriarchal bureaucrat. GOFAI is steered by grand narratives such as the constant development and the control of risks through cyberopticon (Sarafidis, Theodor). Data in GOFAI is processed through representational reductionist models, which are critical for the “management of affairs”. (Beer, Stafford). Liberty AI machines (LAIM) are based on an ecosophic and eudemonic ethos (Beer Stafford, Guattari Felix) that emerges from the viable organization of human affects, emotions, meanings, qualia, representations, intents and actions (Sarafidis). They are constructed as systems (De Angelis, Massimo) by the viable heterarchical organizations of commoners. LAIM are part of machinic phyla (Φ) in open systems or rhizomes (Deleuze & Guattari), operating through a reticulum of the Viable System Model (Beer), the Schizoanalysis (Guattari), the Human Scale Development or Barefoot economics (Max-Neff, Manfred) and Cybersemiotics. LAIM as barefoot machines respect the 'plurality of the commoners' (de Angelis) as autopoietic assemblages of territories of the selves (T), universal references (U), machinic phyla (Φ) and material and signaletic flows (F) (TUΦF). Experts and citizens form participatory networks to produce informational transducers processing “warm datafication” (Bateson, Nora and Massumi, Brian) rather than big datafication. Warm data are transcontextual and transversal diagrams of TUΦF that feed Barefoot AI, setting up “ligne de fuite” to a symbiotic Gaia.

Speaker: Theodor Sarafidis — Department of Social Anthropology, Panteion University, Athens

Room: Room C

sessions.title: Gamifying the VSM
sessions.description:
Purpose: Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model is among the most powerful instruments for diagnosing and designing organisational viability — yet its reach into practice is limited by a high entry threshold: its cybernetic vocabulary and circuit-like notation deter the very people who could benefit most. This project aims to make that dormant potential usable — for civil society, commons, non-profit and for-profit organisations alike — by turning the VSM into a serious game. Methods: It begins with a rearrangement of the five systems, complemented by Angela Espinosa’s Self-Transformation Methodology, into a game design that is built into a digital prototype. Players map their own organisation as connected hexagons, setting them in motion with one minigame per system (1–5), learning the recursive grammar through play rather than instruction. The prototype is tested iteratively with real groups. The pivotal question is how well it helps players become healthier, operationalised through Antonovsky’s Sense of Coherence: comprehensibility, manageability, and meaning. Findings: Expected: whether the VSM, turned into a game, lowers its threshold of entry, and whether playing it strengthens players’ coherence and their organisations’ health. Implications: At its core, Hextech is a new tool for making the VSM applicable — one that finally makes barefoot cybernetics viable in practice, putting self-governance into the hands of those who most need viability yet can least afford its jargon. And it keeps sight of the larger potential dormant in the idea: a polycentric, recursively interwoven network of organisations carrying the seed of a global, recursive consciousness.

Speaker: Sascha Kullak

Room: Room D

sessions.title: Cybernetics For All (#Cybernetics4All)
sessions.description:
Cybernetics, Systems Thinking (Cybersystemics) and, specifically, the VSM, like any topic, can be learned informally or formally. An informal approach is likely to be unstructured and might take the form of using what materials are available, involve trial and error and result in misunderstandings and omissions of key concepts. A formal approach would be expected to be structured in a reasoned way to achieve specific learning outcomes. However, despite Cybernetics being around for over 75 years, there does not appear to be any material that explains how knowledge about Cybernetics, and particularly the VSM, is transferred from teacher to student. What does a course about cybernetics and the VSM look like? This becomes an important question if people want to develop a sound understanding of what constitutes Cybernetics (Cybersystemics). How many people claim to be expert in Cybernetics yet have only a very limited understanding of Cybernetics because it is informally grounded? In response, this paper offers an agenda for a Cybernetics (Cybersystemics) course. Whilst the VSM is the focus, the agenda includes such issues as the contextual background to the VSM, how to use it (VIPLAN method), its ontological implications (real systems or as conceptualisations), which has implications for how it is used in problematic situations (VIPLAN methodology). Since the VSM is not a model for the sake of modelling, but is about how it supports transformation, then this implies that the principles of change management are a necessary topic. Other topics can include its application to teaching research methods, sustainability and (autonomous) technologies. Critical is a language that is understandable. In sum, the agenda is a rich one.

sessions.title: Embracing the Black Box: Why Unexplainable AI (x ̅'AI' ) is a Vital Feature of the Viable System's Algedonic Channel
sessions.description:
The contemporary discourse surrounding Artificial Intelligence governance is dominated by the demand for Explainable AI (XAI), viewing 'black-box' or non-explainable algorithms (x ̅'AI' ) as an inherent systemic risk. This paper challenges that orthodoxy by viewing AI through the lens of Stafford Beer’s Viable System Model (VSM). We argue that the demand for absolute explainability is a violation of Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety, introducing a cognitive bottleneck that forces high-variety ambient data to be aggressively attenuated before it can be utilized. Using modern deep-learning sentiment analysis as a case in point, we demonstrate that x ̅'AI' is not a failure of design, but a potent realization of Beer's algedonic channel. In biological systems, nociception (pain perception) operates as a low-variety, unexplainable emergency signal bypassing conscious cognition to ensure rapid survival. Similarly, x ̅'AI' processing of unstructured customer feedback can detect complex, non-linear emotional shifts across an enterprise’s operational environment. Because these deep learning models operate in high-dimensional spaces, their outputs are fundamentally difficult to serialise into human language. Far from being a liability, this paper posits that x ̅'AI' provides a direct, un-sanitised transduction of environmental variety. When integrated as an algedonic bypass from System 1 directly to System 5, x ̅'AI' alerts leadership to structural threats or opportunities before traditional bureaucratic processes can construct a causal explanation.  Many organizations have already deployed real-time sentiment analysis out of operational necessity, effectively utilizing x ̅'AI' as a de facto algedonic channel. This paper concludes that recognizing these existing systems as cybernetic algedonic loops allows us to better understand their role in organizational survival, framing them not as governance anomalies to be corrected, but as vital mechanisms for maintaining systemic viability.

sessions.title: Languaging an Adaptive Organisation into Existence: from Surprise to Causal Closure
sessions.description:
This abstract reinterprets Stafford Beer's Viable System Model(VSM) as a cybernetic theory of self-perpetuation rather than a managerial framework, grounded explicitly in thermodynamic principle. Beer's long-standing engagement with entropy — signalled by Ludwig Boltzmann's formulation S = k log W and reinforced through direct collaboration and discussion - frames organisational viability as a macro-level phenomenon realised through many micro-level configurations. Viable organisations are thus understood as out-of-equilibrium systems that persist by balancing inevitable entropic decay with continual replenishment drawn from environmental gradients. Organisational identity is treated as a macro-level invariant and a dynamic attractor for value exchange maintained by a boundary interpreted here as a Markov blanket. Within this framing Karl Friston's notion of surprise is understood as an adaptive homeorhetic pressure that steers the system along closure-seeking trajectories without collapse into equilibrium. Owing to the recursive embedding of viable systems surprise is regulated across multiple fractal touchpoints with the environment generating emergent direction rather than centrally determined goals. Value exchange in the Ricardian sense provides the metabolic coupling through which identity is ultimately validated and replenished and viability is sustained only where the resulting gradient exceeds the organisation’s power budget. Marketing is positioned not as the source of identity, but as the maintenance of its attractive field, sustaining recognisability and facilitating exchange. These ideas are illustrated through reflection on the Payphone Serviceability Problem - a project undertaken with Beer - demonstrating the VSM as an architecture for regulating surprise and sustaining organisational life across scale and time.

Speaker: Steve Brewis — The Infinite Game

sessions.title: The Škofja Loka Passion Play as a Nexus of System, Culture, Art and Religion
sessions.description:
Purpose: In 'World in Torment: A Time Whose Idea Must Come', Stafford Beer diagnosed a civilisation governed by low-variety ideologies, losing the identities that hold societary units together. The paper asks what cybernetics contributes to interpreting the Škofja Loka Passion Play – the oldest preserved dramatic text in Slovenian, inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2016. Cybernetics renders visible the structural conditions of the Play’s three-hundred-year viability; the Play is a living counter-example to the torment. Methods: The stance is stated plainly. The Viable System Model (VSM) belongs to organisational cybernetics; a passion play is not a firm. Nothing is prescribed. It is applied as Beer applies it in World in Torment – to any societary unit, “a village or a company, a state or the whole of humankind” – as a diagnostic instrument for evaluating identity, that “highly complex ethos of self-recognition”. A hermeneutic reading of the Play as cultural-spiritual text disciplines the cybernetic one; a case study maps actors, roles and flows. Findings: The study shows that the Škofja Loka Passion Play can be read through the lens of Beer’s Viable System Model. The scenes and processions correspond to the operational level of System 1, while the municipality, local associations, and the monastery jointly assume the coordinating and managerial roles of Systems 2 and 3. Scholarly engagement with the Play functions as System 4, and the religious tradition surrounding it fulfils the System 5 role of articulating and maintaining collective identity. With the involvement of roughly 1,500 volunteers, the production offers abundant leadership potential and, instead of sidelining parts of the community, brings a wide spectrum of people into meaningful participation, countering typical patterns of social exclusion. Implications/contribution: In contrast to enterprise diagnosis (Espejo, Schwaninger, Pérez Ríos, Hoverstadt) and community applications (Leonard; Espinosa and Walker), the paper extends the World in Torment reading of identity to living heritage and the scenic arts – where the idea whose time must come has quietly been coming for three centuries.

sessions.title: Toward viability: applying the Viable System Model to the cruise shorescape
sessions.description:
Cruise tourism stands at a crossroads between two distinct future scenarios. The first scenario mirrors the situation in Venice: a ban on cruise ships, dissatisfied residents, degraded areas, and a loss of authenticity due to visitor pressure (Milano, 2018; Vianello, 2016). The second scenario leads to destination managment that still has enough time to intorduce the regenerative governance (Bellato et al., 2022; Cave and Dredge, 2020). The difference between these two scenarios lies in whether the management of the system matches the complexity of the system it is attempting to manage (Yeoman, 2012).  This paper advocates the view that tourism in Mediterranean cruise destinations is a failure of regulation rather than a problem of capacity. As per Ashby (1956), this is a matter of a variety mismatch. Regulatory variety is at odds with fragmented destination management and fails to keep pace with the variety generated by cruise tourism. This shortfall manifests as bottlenecks, negative reactions from residents, and reactive bans. Each port is caught between the impulses to promote and to restrict, reacts too slowly, and struggles to coordinate activities (Satta et al., 2015; Pechlaner et al., 2014). The bottleneck lies in the organisational structure, not in port infrastructure or destination capacity (Papathanassis, 2025; Barile & Saviano, 2015).  RQ1: Which functions of the VSM are absent or pathological in the cruise shorescape?  RQ2: What variety engineering would render the cruise shorescape viable?

sessions.title: Viable for Whom? Contested Identity in the VSM
sessions.description:
Purpose: The Viable System Model identifies cybernetic characteristics needed for a viable system. The research explores situations in which e several actors with distinct identities and viable systems share a contested situation. The research asks, “Viable for whom?”, a structural question that shapes how the VSM is applied and which ethical frameworks apply. Methods: This analysis of VSM in multi-actor situations uses the axioms of Variety Dynamics, a non-causal framework extending Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety. It distinguishes systems, with a single identity, and the usual application of VSM, from situations, with multiple contested organisational identities. The analysis explores VSM’s potential roles in managing variety across actors in a situation, and the locus of power. Findings: In a contested situation, viability for one entity can attenuate variety and power available to others. Whether a viable whole amplifies or attenuates a part’s variety, and whether changes to viability of a single entity changes the whole’s identity, are key understandings from VSM in this realm. Questions of authoritarianism and emancipation are revealed. Centre–periphery governance arrangements illustrate this. Implications: This presentation extends organisational cybernetics into contested situations, where viability irregularly spans individual entities and the whole. VSM’s boundaries in the larger world are revealed and extended by viewing such VSM situations through the lens of Variety Dynamics. Beer expressed his concern about a world in torment. Variety Dynamics extends his understandings onto the terrain that produces that torment.

sessions.title: Gameful Experiences for Hopeful Futures: CyberNations
sessions.description:
'If that Cybernetics stuff is so valuable, why don’t you teach it in primary school?'' This provocation started the Gameful Experiences for Hopeful Futures program at the Australian National University School of Cybernetics. How do we teach organisational cybernetics to broader and younger audiences, using creative pedagogies? How do we build practices that embed into our ways of thinking and doing what Stafford called the 'holistic message [of cybernetics]: a science of the regulation of large, complex, probabilistic systems actually exists that is interdisciplinary in approach and consequently inclusive in its world view.' This (ideally 2-hour but adaptable) interactive workshop offers three gameful steps into these questions. First, a short choose-your-own-adventure presentation, in which the audience steers the speaker through an introductory exploration of cybernetics, games, and culture. Second, a facilitated playthrough of CyberNations: an experiment in teaching cybernetic futures in classrooms and board rooms through a semi-cooperative, persistent board game. Inspired by Stafford’s work and Australian First Nations ways of knowing and being, CyberNations teaches core concepts of systems dynamics, requisite variety, intergenerational responsibility, and the fundamental structural coupling between societies and environments. Third, a facilitated debriefing reflecting on the experience, inviting the audience to challenge and contribute to the model. This workshop and its components have been iteratively developed through deliveries in Australian classrooms, playrooms and team-building exercises, espousing Metaphorum’s values of critical, creative and collaborative re-invention. It may interest researchers, educators and practitioners interested in the contribution that game-based learning could make to the Barefoot Cybernetics agenda.

sessions.title: Midlife Chrysalis: from ‘good Chinese boy’ and economics to Stafford Beer-aholics
sessions.description:
From expert economic witness testifying and citing The Nature of the Firm (Coase) to courts and antitrust regulators in high-stakes litigation; to discombobulated PhD student interpreting The Brain of the Firm (Beer) to diagnose ‘System 3*s’ in green building rating organisations. I reflect on my transition from ‘a good Chinese boy’ gainfully employed as a policy/regulatory economist advising on ‘optimal pathways’, to liquefying my DNA inside an untested transdisciplinary chrysalis, to the throes of turning cybernetic and learning to accept: ‘no hay camino, se hace camino al andar.’ [there is no road; you make your own path as you walk.] Somewhere along the way—between piloting the Master of Applied Cybernetics at the Australian National University (ANU), watching my country in flames, starting a cohort based PhD programme, locking down amidst a global pandemic and drafting a research agenda for a new School of Cybernetics (SOCY)—I stumbled into Stafford Beer. The Viable System Model (VSM) is now core to my research to develop new theory and praxis on viable sociotechnical/sustainability transition intermediary organisations for transforming our buildings and cities. As the School’s de facto Chief Beer Officer (CBO), I will also celebrate some new research from fellow travellers also inspired by Stafford Beer. SOCY PhD students who have adopted and adapted the Viable System Model (VSM) to generate novel insights for how to viably manage sociotechnical systems, such as ‘smart’ street lighting infrastructure, and decision making structures of early-stage venture capital firms in the age of AI.

sessions.title: Diagnosing the System of the Self: Logical Closure, Normative Identity, and Existential Viability
sessions.description:
The self is increasingly understood as a process rather than a static substance. Consequently, the question is no longer what the self is, but what organizational function it performs and how it remains viable over time. Drawing on Stafford Beer's Viable System Model, I argue that the self performs the function Beer assigns to an ideal System Five: providing logical closure by regulating the interaction between present organization (System Three) and future adaptation (System Four) according to a normative identity. Whereas autopoietic systems regulate toward ultrastability, selves regulate toward existentially normative identities that prescribe who they ought to become. Human viability therefore depends not merely on organizational coherence but on sustaining a normative identity that continually expands the horizon of viable possibilities.  I argue that this norm is not environmentally determined but generated through the continual reorganization of experience into interpretive structures that enlarge the horizon of meaningful action. Thus, the self functions as a minimal model that transduces lived experience and future possibilities into these structures while preserving continuity with an evolving identity. Meaning is the normative significance possibilities acquire within that identity. Logical closure is therefore directed not simply toward survival but toward preserving the conditions for continued meaningful becoming.  This framework offers a cybernetic-existential reinterpretation of psychopathology. Disorders of the self arise when logical closure either collapses, severing meaningful engagement with future possibilities, or becomes pathological by reducing identity to rigid self-preservation. This reinterpretation establishes a conceptual bridge between organizational cybernetics, philosophy of selfhood, and existential psychopathology.

sessions.title: From Organisation to State: Adapting, Reinterpreting and Challenging Stafford Beer’s Cybernetic Ideas in Public Administration and Democratic Governance — The Case of URUCIB in Uruguay
sessions.description:
Purpose: Stafford Beer developed the Viable System Model (VSM) primarily for complex organisations in industrial and managerial contexts. This paper examines what happens when Beer’s cybernetic framework is applied — for the first time under fully democratic conditions — to the challenge of governing a nation-state, using URUCIB (URUguay CIBernético), a real-time executive information system implemented at the Presidency of Uruguay (1985–1992), as its primary case. Methods: The paper draws on the author’s firsthand account as URUCIB’s project director, on primary documents (presidential resolutions, internal memoranda, UNDP project reports, and correspondence with Beer), and on subsequent academic publications about the project. It applies a comparative analytical framework, contrasting Beer’s original VSM assumptions with the structural realities encountered in democratic public administration. Findings: Six critical dimensions required adaptation or challenge: (1) System Five must be reconceptualised around democratic legitimacy rather than managerial authority; (2) the VSM’s diagnostic power is limited in institutionally fragmented bureaucracies; (3) the black-box control paradigm is insufficient for democratic governance, where contextual human judgment is irreducible; (4) institutional trust functions as a cybernetic variable; (5) public organisations resist redesign through autopoietic self-reproduction; and (6) algedonic feedback channels do not adequately capture the political agency of democratic citizens. Implications/contributions: The paper introduces the concept of democratic viability — the capacity to maintain operational effectiveness while simultaneously preserving legitimacy, plurality, and accountability — as a necessary extension of Beer’s organisational viability for governmental contexts. It argues that URUCIB, though pre-internet, directly anticipates contemporary debates on digital governance, algorithmic decision-making, and AI in public administration. The core lesson: governance cybernetics is always also a political and ethical challenge, inseparable from the technical one.

sessions.title: Translating VSM into Practice: A Capability‑Led Approach using Microsoft 365
sessions.description:
This presentation introduces an approach to operationalising Stafford Beer’s Viable Systems Model (VSM) through a capability-led system design supported by contemporary digital infrastructure. Educational organisations operating in complex environments with distributed roles, multiple stakeholders, and regulatory requirements often encounter fragmentation, inconsistent practices, and challenges in achieving coordination and coherence. These issues are particularly visible in contexts where compliance and quality assurance expectations shape operational practice. The approach begins with the development of a four-pillar capability framework that defines the key requirements for effective system functioning within a department: operational practice, capability development, resource utilisation, and organisational resilience. This framework provides a structured basis for supporting consistent and sustainable performance across teams. To organise these four pillars at a system level, the framework is operationalised through VSM, with its elements divided into workstreams that form the operational units, supported by system-level coordination and management. This is further translated into an operational architecture using the Microsoft 365 ecosystem, embedding communication, monitoring, coordination, compliance visibility, and governance within tools such as Teams, Planner, SharePoint, Lists, Power BI, and Power Automate. The model demonstrates how individual workstreams can operate with autonomy while remaining aligned within a coherent system structure, enabled through a Microsoft 365 environment. While informed by experience in educational organisations and compliance-driven environments, the approach is transferable across complex organisational settings. It introduces clarity to system structure to support coordination, demonstrating how systems thinking can be translated into practical organisational design

sessions.title: Governance in the Magdalena River Community from the Postulates of the Viable System Model
sessions.description:
The current problems facing humanity are closely linked to entropy in social-ecological systems, particularly because these systems are embedded within highly complex environments. This is especially evident in territories of high environmental value, where communities manage these areas empirically or through ancestral knowledge. Presently, in Mexico City, there remains a last river (Magdalena) located within a conservation zone that partially supplies potable water to the surrounding communities. This research aims to diagnose the social-ecological system existing in the Magdalena River area through the Viable System Model (VSM). The results show that applying the VSM to unstructured (rigid) rural communities enables an understanding of the system’s “living” state and its main weaknesses, which are driven by urban sprawl pollution and overtourism, primarily impacting System 5. This indicates that System 5 is overloaded by external disturbances that Systems 1-4 fail to absorb. This implies that the rural community’s identity has become exposed, lacking the necessary recursivity to address its viability in the face of such disturbances. Should System 5 collapse or lose its identity, the entire system ceases to exist as a viable unit. It is proposed to equip the system with recursive mechanisms that allow it to filter urban pressure and redefine its identity from autonomy rather than reaction. Through this, the Magdalena River can cease to be an “object,” gaining the capacity to generate an identity that provides homeostatic balance to the entire system and its environment.

sessions.title: Rethinking Organisational Networks: Practical Insights from Applying the Viable System Model in Real World Ecosystems
sessions.description:
Purpose: Organizational networks are often approached as if they were conventional organizations, despite their fundamentally different nature. Drawing on our work with more than 20 networks across mental health care, palliative care, youth care, mobility, circular economy, and labour market integration, this presentation shows how the Viable System Model (VSM) helps networks understand their identity, governance, and contribution within larger ecosystems. Methods: Using case examples throughout, we present a practice-based approach developed through long-term coaching, training, and facilitation. VSM is applied across multiple recursion levels by distinguishing the network as ecosystem, the network as a bounded partnership, and the network as an organization. This perspective supports governance design, stakeholder engagement, and strategic development. Findings: Illustrated by cases from different sectors, we show how confusion between recursion levels often leads to misunderstandings about governance, responsibilities, and purpose. VSM enables participants to distinguish these perspectives, creating a shared understanding of the network's identity and role. This, in turn, supports richer strategic conversations about the network's intended contribution, strengthens collaboration among partners, and increases engagement across the network. Implications/Contributions: By grounding conceptual insights in diverse practice cases, the presentation demonstrates how VSM can be effectively applied to organizational networks and offers researchers and practitioners practical approaches for diagnosing, designing, and developing viable multi-organizational collaborations.

sessions.title: From Building a Regime to Running It: A Participatory Viable System Model Diagnostic of a Regulator Entering Dual-Mode Operation
sessions.description:
Purpose: In January 2026 the Heat Networks Directorate of Ofgem moved from designing a new regulatory regime to operating it while continuing to develop it. Initially our project asked how they could develop a better operating model, but what it concluded was that they were shifting to from a single to two core activities and needed to adapt to be able to deliver in parallel. Methods: Over ten weeks the authors combined an independent diagnostic with certified Practitioner training. A preliminary recursive map, developed inside the Directorate through a Royal Academy of Engineering Policy Fellowship, became the training material: seven staff qualified as Practitioners while jointly interrogating and revising their own model. Four systems were analysed across three levels of recursion. Findings: The decisive finding was structural. Operating the regime and developing it can no longer share one management system; each needs its own delivery, coordination and adaptive capacity, introducing a new level of recursion at the top. The analysis produced 108 observations and 28 mitigations, concentrated in under-developed coordination (System 2), thin adaptation (System 4) and an absent technical authority. sessions.title: From Values to Organizational Practice - the Contribution of the VSM to value-oriented leadership in the age of digitalization
sessions.description:
New technologies create ambivalence. In these times of upheaval, values and ethics are needed as stabilizing forces and guides. Building on the VSM, this contribution explores some of the key organizational mechanisms that value-oriented leadership should focus on to ensure that it does not remain abstract but is actually reflected in the concrete actions and decisions of organizations. The VSM hereby reveals its particular strength: offering multi-faceted and detailed insights while preserving an overarching frame of reference. In addition to the organizational dimension of value-oriented leadership, this article derives from the VSM and the underlying Ashby’s Law an ethical imperative as well as guidelines for an ethical decision-making process.

sessions.title: Diagnosing the System for Systems Research: Recognising and Realising a Field in Itself and for Itself (keynote)
sessions.description:
Stafford Beer gave the world an instrument for diagnosing viability. A hundred years on, the field that carries his name has rarely turned that instrument on itself. The 2026 agenda of the International Federation for Systems Research reads the cyber-systemic field as vibrant and dispersed: ten clusters of inquiry, wide application, thin synthesis, and a scarcity of the very self-reflection the field so readily prescribes to others. A success paradox running into a reflexivity gap. Read cybernetically, the diagnosis becomes uncomfortably familiar. A proliferating System One that seldom cross-pollinates. A System Four holding no outside-and-then. A System Five never articulated, so that identity is inherited rather than chosen. And the question that will not let go: where are the algedonic signals of the field, and to whom do they speak? Any answer already presumes a we. This keynote offers an invitation to co-create the conditions for a joint learning journey, and to ground collective agency in the field's sense of we.

sessions.title: Reconstruction of the Cybersyn Operating Room
sessions.description:
This article and photo essay will present the history and international impact of the reconstruction of the Cybersyn operating room, conceived by Stafford Beer, designed by the INTEC Industrial Design Department in 1973, and reconstructed 50 years later for the exhibition “How to Design a Revolution: The Chilean Path to Design,” a show about graphic and industrial design during the government of Salvador Allende in Chile. The exhibition was conceived through the interdisciplinary research and creative work of professors from the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the United States. This exhibition was inaugurated at the La Moneda Cultural Center in Santiago, Chile, between 2023 and 2024, to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the civil-military coup d'état. It was later presented at the Disseny Hub in Barcelona in 2025. This exhibition will be held between 2026 and 2027 at the Museum Angewandte Kunst in Frankfurt as part of the World Design Capital Frankfurt 2026 event. The exhibition comprises design pieces that aimed to democratize reading and music, reduce technological dependence, and combat childhood malnutrition, among other goals. One of the most outstanding pieces in the exhibition is the first comprehensive and functional reconstruction of the Cybersyn operating room. This article offers a visual account of the journeys that made the reconstruction of this project possible—a milestone in the history of design and cybernetics with which exhibition visitors can now interact.
